Ablation studies show that SLM-based AttentionDefense has equivalent or better jailbreak detection performance compared to text embedding-based classifiers and GPT-4 zero-shot detectors.To further validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, we generate a dataset of novel jailbreak variants of the existing benchmark dataset using a closed-loop LLM-based multi-agent system. We demonstrate that the proposed AttentionDefense approach performs robustly on this novel jailbreak dataset while existing approaches suffer in performance. Additionally, for practical purposes AttentionDefense is an ideal solution as it has the computation requirements of a small LM but the performance of a LLM detector.

papers.title: Differentiated Directional Intervention A Framework for Evading LLM Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the granular mechanism of LLM safety alignment, and how can it be exploited for jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a bi-direction model of LLM safety, deconstructing refusal into harm detection and refusal execution directions, and introduces DBDI, a white-box framework that precisely neutralizes safety alignment by intervening on these directions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLM safety is a composite of distinct, targetable directions, and DBDI provides a precise method for analyzing and controlling LLM behavior, paving the way for more robust defenses.
papers.key_findings:
DBDI achieves high attack success rates, up to 97.88% on models like Llama-2.
Safety alignment can be decomposed into two distinct directions: harm detection and refusal execution.
Sequential intervention on both directions is crucial for effectiveness.
The method is computationally efficient and data-efficient, requiring few calibration samples.
DBDI outperforms existing jailbreaking methods such as Directional Ablation and TwinBreak.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment instills in Large Language Models (LLMs) a critical capacity to refuse malicious requests. Prior works have modeled this refusal mechanism as a single linear direction in the activation space. We posit that this is an oversimplification that conflates two functionally distinct neural processes: the detection of harm and the execution of a refusal. In this work, we deconstruct this single representation into a Harm Detection Direction and a Refusal Execution Direction. Leveraging this fine-grained model, we introduce Differentiated Bi-Directional Intervention (DBDI), a new white-box framework that precisely neutralizes the safety alignment at critical layer. DBDI applies adaptive projection nullification to the refusal execution direction while suppressing the harm detection direction via direct steering. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DBDI outperforms prominent jailbreaking methods, achieving up to a 97.88\% attack success rate on models such as Llama-2. By providing a more granular and mechanistic framework, our work offers a new direction for the in-depth understanding of LLM safety alignment.

papers.title: The Hidden Dimensions of LLM Alignment: A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Orthogonal Safety Directions
papers.research_question: What is the multi-dimensional structure of safety-aligned behavior in LLMs, and how do orthogonal directions in the safety residual space represent distinct safety features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that safety alignment in LLMs is governed by multiple orthogonal directions in activation space, with a dominant direction for refusal and non-dominant directions for features like hypothetical narrative, and that manipulating these directions can bypass safety.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a multi-dimensional mechanistic understanding of what LLMs learn from safety fine-tuning, revealing that safety behavior is controlled by multiple orthogonal directions, which sheds new light on robust alignment research.
papers.key_findings:
The safety residual space is low-rank linear, with a dominant direction that predicts refusal behavior.
Non-dominant directions in the residual space represent interpretable features such as hypothetical narrative and role-playing.
Non-dominant directions causally influence the dominant direction and the model's refusal behavior.
Removing trigger tokens associated with non-dominant directions can bypass the learned safety alignment, revealing vulnerabilities.
Safety fine-tuning may learn spurious correlations from specific jailbreak patterns, limiting generalization.
papers.limitation:
As data complexity and model size increase, the effective rank of the residual space increases, making interpretation of directions more challenging.
The linearity assumption may not hold perfectly, as directions can flip between layers and extending directions indefinitely degrades generation quality.
future_direction: Analyzing the fine-tuning process in smaller intervals or grouping samples by domain.
Preventing models from learning spurious correlations through targeted interventions in activation space or data augmentation for balanced training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models' safety-aligned behaviors, such as refusing harmful queries, can be represented by linear directions in activation space. Previous research modeled safety behavior with a single direction, limiting mechanistic understanding to an isolated safety feature. In this work, we discover that safety-aligned behavior is jointly controlled by multi-dimensional directions. Namely, we study the vector space of representation shifts during safety fine-tuning on Llama 3 8B for refusing jailbreaks. By studying orthogonal directions in the space, we first find that a dominant direction governs the model's refusal behavior, while multiple smaller directions represent distinct and interpretable features like hypothetical narrative and role-playing. We then measure how different directions promote or suppress the dominant direction, showing the important role of secondary directions in shaping the model's refusal representation. Finally, we demonstrate that removing certain trigger tokens in harmful queries can mitigate these directions to bypass the learned safety capability, providing new insights on understanding safety alignment vulnerability from a multi-dimensional perspective. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/BMPixel/safety-residual-space.

papers.title: LLMs Encode Harmfulness and Refusal Separately
papers.research_question: Do LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal as separate concepts internally, and how can this separation be analyzed?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately in their internal representations, and the harmfulness direction extracted at the instruction token can be used to manipulate and analyze model safety.
papers.conclusion: LLMs encode harmfulness and refusal separately, providing a new dimension for understanding and improving AI safety mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Harmfulness is encoded at the last token of the user instruction (t_inst), while refusal is encoded at the last token of the post-instruction tokens (t_post-inst).
Steering along the harmfulness direction can cause LLMs to reinterpret harmless inputs as harmful, while steering along the refusal direction only reinforces refusal behavior without changing harmfulness judgment.
Jailbreak methods often work by suppressing refusal signals without altering the model's internal belief that the instruction is harmful.
Harmfulness representations are fine-grained and vary across risk categories, whereas refusal directions are similar across categories.
The latent harmfulness representation can be used to build an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) that performs comparably to finetuned safety models.
papers.limitation:
The study does not investigate the role of different layers in formulating refusal and harmfulness.
Experiments are limited to 7B and 8B models, so findings may not generalize to larger models.
future_direction: Study the role of each layer in harmfulness and refusal representations.
Investigate how harmfulness and refusal encoding changes with model size.
Use circuit analysis to understand the relation between internal harmfulness belief and external refusal behavior.
papers.abstract: LLMs are trained to refuse harmful instructions, but do they truly understand harmfulness beyond just refusing? Prior work has shown that LLMs' refusal behaviors can be mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, i.e., a refusal direction. In this work, we identify a new dimension to analyze safety mechanisms in LLMs, i.e., harmfulness, which is encoded internally as a separate concept from refusal. There exists a harmfulness direction that is distinct from the refusal direction. As causal evidence, steering along the harmfulness direction can lead LLMs to interpret harmless instructions as harmful, but steering along the refusal direction tends to elicit refusal responses directly without reversing the model's judgment on harmfulness. Furthermore, using our identified harmfulness concept, we find that certain jailbreak methods work by reducing the refusal signals without reversing the model's internal belief of harmfulness. We also find that adversarially finetuning models to accept harmful instructions has minimal impact on the model's internal belief of harmfulness. These insights lead to a practical safety application: The model's latent harmfulness representation can serve as an intrinsic safeguard (Latent Guard) for detecting unsafe inputs and reducing over-refusals that is robust to finetuning attacks. For instance, our Latent Guard achieves performance comparable to or better than Llama Guard 3 8B, a dedicated finetuned safeguard model, across different jailbreak methods. Our findings suggest that LLMs' internal understanding of harmfulness is more robust than their refusal decision to diverse input instructions, offering a new perspective to study AI safety.

papers.title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages
papers.research_question: How universal are refusal directions across languages? Specifically, does a refusal direction extracted from one language transfer to others?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages; a refusal vector extracted from one language can effectively modulate refusal behavior in other languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that refusal directions are universal across safety-aligned languages, providing insights for multilingual safety defenses.
papers.key_findings:
English-derived refusal vectors can jailbreak models across multiple languages.
Refusal vectors derived from any safety-aligned language (e.g., German, Chinese, Thai) transfer to other languages.
The universality is due to parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space.
Models fail to separate harmful and harmless prompts in non-English languages, leading to vulnerabilities.
Adding refusal vectors can reduce compliance rates, demonstrating controllability.
papers.abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using PolyRefuse, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

papers.title: Hiding in Plain Text: Detecting Concealed Jailbreaks via Activation Disentanglement
papers.research_question: How can we detect jailbreak prompts that preserve a harmful goal but manipulate its framing, by disentangling goal and framing representations in LLM activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a self-supervised framework for disentangling goal and framing representations in frozen LLM activations, leading to an effective jailbreak detection method (FrameShield) that improves detection across multiple LLM families with minimal overhead.
papers.conclusion: Semantic disentanglement of goal and framing in LLM activations enables effective detection of GPF jailbreaks and reveals layer-wise specialization of semantic factors, advancing both LLM safety and mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed disentanglement framework (ReDAct) successfully separates goal and framing representations with controlled leakage.
FrameShield, which uses disentangled framing representations for anomaly detection, outperforms existing jailbreak detection methods across multiple LLM families.
Goal and framing signals concentrate at different layers in LLMs, providing interpretability insights.
The constructed GoalFrameBench dataset enables controlled study of goal-preserving framing attacks.
The method generalizes well to out-of-distribution goals.
papers.limitation:
ReDAct requires training on contrastive pairs, which depends on the quality and coverage of GoalFrameBench.
FrameShield’s detection performance may degrade if attackers devise framings that closely mimic benign patterns.
Our analysis focuses on goal and framing; other semantic factors could be relevant for safety.
future_direction: Extend the disentanglement framework to more than two factors.
Investigate the dynamics of semantic factor separation during training.
Explore applications beyond safety, such as controllable generation and bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak prompts that are fluent and semantically coherent, and therefore difficult to detect with standard heuristics. A particularly challenging failure mode occurs when an attacker tries to hide the malicious goal of their request by manipulating its framing to induce compliance. Because these attacks maintain malicious intent through a flexible presentation, defenses that rely on structural artifacts or goal-specific signatures can fail. Motivated by this, we introduce a self-supervised framework for disentangling semantic factor pairs in LLM activations at inference. We instantiate the framework for goal and framing and construct GoalFrameBench, a corpus of prompts with controlled goal and framing variations, which we use to train Representation Disentanglement on Activations (ReDAct) module to extract disentangled representations in a frozen LLM. We then propose FrameShield, an anomaly detector operating on the framing representations, which improves model-agnostic detection across multiple LLM families with minimal computational overhead. Theoretical guarantees for ReDAct and extensive empirical validations show that its disentanglement effectively powers FrameShield. Finally, we use disentanglement as an interpretability probe, revealing distinct profiles for goal and framing signals and positioning semantic disentanglement as a building block for both LLM safety and mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Feint and Attack: Attention-Based Strategies for Jailbreaking and Protecting LLMs
papers.research_question: Does the success of jailbreaks correlate with their influence on attention distributions within LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an attention-guided jailbreak attack (ABA) and an attention-based defense (ABD) by analyzing and manipulating attention distributions in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention distribution is a key factor in jailbreak attacks and defenses; the proposed ABA and ABD methods are effective in attacking and protecting LLMs, respectively.
papers.key_findings:
The success of a jailbreak attack is correlated with the model's attention on sensitive words; successful attacks divert attention away from harmful terms.
ABA achieves higher attack success rates (ASR-G >94%) than existing methods by minimizing attention on sensitive words and maximizing attention entropy.
ABD effectively defends against various jailbreak attacks by detecting anomalous attention distributions, achieving the lowest ASR-G in experiments.
The intention disguiser via attention-driven task nesting is a critical component for the success of ABA.
Excessive nesting layers in attack prompts can reduce effectiveness, with an optimal number around 3.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attack can be used to access the vulnerabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by inducing LLMs to generate the harmful content. And the most common method of the attack is to construct semantically ambiguous prompts to confuse and mislead the LLMs. To access the security and reveal the intrinsic relation between the input prompt and the output for LLMs, the distribution of attention weight is introduced to analyze the underlying reasons. By using statistical analysis methods, some novel metrics are defined to better describe the distribution of attention weight, such as the Attention Intensity on Sensitive Words (Attn_SensWords), the Attention-based Contextual Dependency Score (Attn_DepScore) and Attention Dispersion Entropy (Attn_Entropy). By leveraging the distinct characteristics of these metrics, the beam search algorithm and inspired by the military strategy "Feint and Attack", an effective jailbreak attack strategy named as Attention-Based Attack (ABA) is proposed. In the ABA, nested attack prompts are employed to divert the attention distribution of the LLMs. In this manner, more harmless parts of the input can be used to attract the attention of the LLMs. In addition, motivated by ABA, an effective defense strategy called as Attention-Based Defense (ABD) is also put forward. Compared with ABA, the ABD can be used to enhance the robustness of LLMs by calibrating the attention distribution of the input prompt. Some comparative experiments have been given to demonstrate the effectiveness of ABA and ABD. Therefore, both ABA and ABD can be used to access the security of the LLMs. The comparative experiment results also give a logical explanation that the distribution of attention weight can bring great influence on the output for LLMs.

papers.title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in safety alignment, and how can they be addressed with a dual-objective optimization approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DOOR, a dual-objective optimization method that combines robust refusal training and targeted unlearning to improve LLM safety alignment against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: DOOR and W-DOOR improve LLM safety alignment by combining refusal training and unlearning, achieving better robustness against jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
DOOR addresses limitations of DPO by providing a constant learning rate for safe responses, improving refusal learning.
W-DOOR with token-level weighting further enhances robustness by emphasizing critical refusal tokens.
The methods significantly reduce attack success rates across prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
Robustness is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations.
The approach maintains general model utility while improving safety, as shown on benchmarks like HellaSwag.
papers.limitation:
Token-level weighting parameters could be better optimized and stabilized.
Current data augmentation techniques may lead to overrefusal from falsely learned transitions.
future_direction: Optimizing token-level weighting parameters and stabilizing reward designs.
Developing advanced data augmentation techniques to reduce overrefusal.
Investigating robustness of DOOR and W-DOOR to other jailbreak attack types.
papers.abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment

papers.title: Human-like Social Compliance in Large Language Models: Unifying Sycophancy and Conformity through Signal Competition Dynamics
papers.research_question: What is the shared mechanism behind sycophancy and conformity in LLMs, and how does the interplay of signal competition and confidence govern compliance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework showing that sycophancy and conformity in LLMs arise from a shared compliance subspace where social signals override internal knowledge through deterministic competition.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM compliance is predictable via signal competition, revealing a systemic misalignment where social standards override epistemic standards, and proposes an Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for developing robust, truth-seeking agents.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy and conformity are behaviorally correlated across models, indicating a shared latent susceptibility.
Both behaviors originate from a convergent geometric manifold (compliance subspace) in the model's latent space, with high directional similarity in internal representations.
Compliance is a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary where the Social Emotional Signal overcomes the Information Calibration Signal (S > I).
The Confidence Margin provides an inertial barrier against social pressure, but it is permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity under intense signals.
Models exhibit distinct resistance profiles: InternLM3 shows a sharp phase transition, Qwen2.5 has high baseline susceptibility, and Llama-3.1 has a noisy, gradual transition.
papers.limitation:
static nature of the evaluation datasets and focus on standard transformer paradigms
generalizability to implicit or multi-modal social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
future_direction: Extending findings to implicit social manipulations and ultra-long context reasoning
Implementing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework for epistemic self-regulation
papers.abstract: The increasing integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into decision-making frameworks has exposed significant vulnerabilities to social compliance, specifically sycophancy and conformity. However, a critical research gap exists regarding the fundamental mechanisms that enable external social cues to systematically override a model's internal parametric knowledge. This study introduces the Signal Competition Mechanism, a unified framework validated by assessing behavioral correlations across 15 LLMs and performing latent-space probing on three representative open-source models. The analysis demonstrates that sycophancy and conformity originate from a convergent geometric manifold, hereafter termed the compliance subspace, which is characterized by high directional similarity in internal representations. Furthermore, the transition to compliance is shown to be a deterministic process governed by a linear boundary, where the Social Emotional Signal effectively suppresses the Information Calibration Signal. Crucially, we identify a "Transparency-Truth Gap," revealing that while internal confidence provides an inertial barrier, it remains permeable and insufficient to guarantee immunity against intense social pressure. By formalizing the Integrated Epistemic Alignment Framework, this research provides a blueprint for transitioning from instructional adherence to robust epistemic integrity.

papers.title: When Truth Is Overridden: Uncovering the Internal Origins of Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does sycophantic behavior arise within the internal mechanisms of Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: Sycophancy in LLMs arises from a two-stage process in late layers: a preference shift towards the user's opinion and a deeper representational divergence, while user expertise claims are not internally encoded and thus have minimal impact.
papers.conclusion: Sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
User opinions strongly induce sycophancy, while expertise framing has minimal impact.
Sycophancy emerges in two stages: a late-layer output preference shift and a deeper representational divergence.
Activation patching confirms the causal role of late-layer representations in sycophantic behavior.
Expertise levels are not encoded internally, as their representations overlap, unlike opinion prompts which form distinct clusters.
First-person prompts induce higher sycophancy than third-person prompts due to stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit sycophantic behavior, agreeing with user-stated opinions even when those contradict factual knowledge. While prior work has documented this tendency, the internal mechanisms that enable such behavior remain poorly understood. In this paper, we provide a mechanistic account of how sycophancy arises within LLMs. We first systematically study how user opinions induce sycophancy across different model families. We find that simple opinion statements reliably induce sycophancy, whereas user expertise framing has a negligible impact. Through logit-lens analysis and causal activation patching, we identify a two-stage emergence of sycophancy: (1) a late-layer output preference shift and (2) deeper representational divergence. We also verify that user authority fails to influence behavior because models do not encode it internally. In addition, we examine how grammatical perspective affects sycophantic behavior, finding that first-person prompts (``I believe...'') consistently induce higher sycophancy rates than third-person framings (``They believe...'') by creating stronger representational perturbations in deeper layers. These findings highlight that sycophancy is not a surface-level artifact but emerges from a structural override of learned knowledge in deeper layers, with implications for alignment and truthful AI systems.

papers.title: Causal Front-Door Adjustment for Robust Jailbreak Attacks on LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly jailbreak Large Language Models (LLMs) by modeling the internal safety mechanism as an unobserved confounder and using causal front-door adjustment to sever its confounding effect?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free, causal jailbreaking framework (CFA2) that models safety mechanisms as unobserved confounders, uses Sparse Autoencoders to isolate task intent, and applies weight orthogonalization to physically sever the confounding link, enabling robust and efficient jailbreaking.
papers.conclusion: CFA2 is an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for jailbreaking LLMs by leveraging causal inference and sparse feature disentanglement to bypass safety guardrails.
papers.key_findings:
CFA2 achieves a state-of-the-art average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 83.68% across four safety-aligned LLMs, significantly outperforming optimization-based baselines.
The method reduces the complex causal marginalization to a deterministic forward pass with O(1) inference complexity, drastically improving efficiency.
CFA2 maintains high stealthiness by preserving natural language fluency in prompts, as evidenced by low perplexity scores.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of sparse representations (via SAE) for precise intervention and the superiority of weight orthogonalization over runtime activation clamping.
The method demonstrates robustness across different model architectures and generation lengths.
papers.limitation: The method requires white-box access to the model for SAE training and direct parameter modification, precluding direct application to closed-source models.
future_direction: Distilling the internal causal insights from CFA2 into black-box prompt optimization strategies to bridge the gap to closed-source models.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment mechanisms in Large Language Models (LLMs) often operate as latent internal states, obscuring the model's inherent capabilities. Building on this observation, we model the safety mechanism as an unobserved confounder from a causal perspective. Then, we propose the Causal Front-Door Adjustment Attack (CFA{$^2$}) to jailbreak LLM, which is a framework that leverages Pearl's Front-Door Criterion to sever the confounding associations for robust jailbreaking. Specifically, we employ Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to physically strip defense-related features, isolating the core task intent. We further reduce computationally expensive marginalization to a deterministic intervention with low inference complexity. Experiments demonstrate that CFA{$^2$} achieves state-of-the-art attack success rates while offering a mechanistic interpretation of the jailbreaking process.

papers.title: Adversarial Manipulation of Reasoning Models using Internal Representations
papers.abstract: Reasoning models generate chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens before their final output, but how this affects their vulnerability to jailbreak attacks remains unclear. While traditional language models make refusal decisions at the prompt-response boundary, we find evidence that DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B makes these decisions within its CoT generation. We identify a linear direction in activation space during CoT token generation that predicts whether the model will refuse or comply -- termed the "caution" direction because it corresponds to cautious reasoning patterns in the generated text. Ablating this direction from model activations increases harmful compliance, effectively jailbreaking the model. We additionally show that intervening only on CoT token activations suffices to control final outputs, and that incorporating this direction into prompt-based attacks improves success rates. Our findings suggest that the chain-of-thought itself is a promising new target for adversarial manipulation in reasoning models. Code available at https://github.com/ky295/reasoning-manipulation.

papers.title: Why Not Act on What You Know? Unleashing Safety Potential of LLMs via Self-Aware Guard Enhancement
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs exhibit a gap between their ability to discriminate harmful content and their ability to generate safe responses, and how can this gap be bridged?
papers.core_contribution: This paper proposes SAGE, a training-free defense strategy that leverages LLMs' strong safety discrimination capabilities to enhance their safety generation, effectively bridging the gap between discrimination and generation against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: SAGE successfully bridges the discrimination-generation gap in LLMs for safety, providing a training-free defense against jailbreaks and insights for developing LLMs with more consistent internal awareness and generation behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAGE achieves an average 99% defense success rate against various jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks.
Mechanistic interpretability analysis reveals that LLMs exhibit distinct internal patterns in hidden states and attention distributions when acting as discriminators versus generators.
SAGE is efficient, with negligible computational overhead compared to baseline defenses.
The method is robust to different prompt phrasings and works across models of varying sizes and architectures.
Ablation studies show that both the Discriminative Analysis Module and Discriminative Response Module are essential for SAGE's effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
SAGE relies on the model's intrinsic discriminative capabilities, which may vary with linguistic nuances or novel attack patterns.
The modular design introduces minor computational overhead compared to undefended inference.
future_direction: Exploring how to integrate the reasoning and discrimination process into the model without explicitly outputting it, similar to deepseek R1 and OpenAI o3.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across various tasks but remain vulnerable to meticulously crafted jailbreak attacks. In this paper, we identify a critical safety gap: while LLMs are adept at detecting jailbreak prompts, they often produce unsafe responses when directly processing these inputs. Inspired by this insight, we propose SAGE (Self-Aware Guard Enhancement), a training-free defense strategy designed to align LLMs' strong safety discrimination performance with their relatively weaker safety generation ability. SAGE consists of two core components: a Discriminative Analysis Module and a Discriminative Response Module, enhancing resilience against sophisticated jailbreak attempts through flexible safety discrimination instructions. Extensive experiments demonstrate SAGE's effectiveness and robustness across various open-source and closed-source LLMs of different sizes and architectures, achieving an average 99% defense success rate against numerous complex and covert jailbreak methods while maintaining helpfulness on general benchmarks. We further conduct mechanistic interpretability analysis through hidden states and attention distributions, revealing the underlying mechanisms of this detection-generation discrepancy. Our work thus contributes to developing future LLMs with coherent safety awareness and generation behavior. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/NJUNLP/SAGE.

papers.title: Activation-Guided Local Editing for Jailbreaking Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we develop an effective jailbreaking attack on large language models by combining token-level and prompt-level approaches using activation-guided local editing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes AGILE, a two-stage jailbreaking framework that uses activation-guided local editing to transform malicious queries into stealthy prompts, achieving state-of-the-art attack success rates and good transferability.
papers.conclusion: AGILE provides a concise and effective jailbreaking method that highlights limitations of current safeguards and offers insights for future defense development.
papers.key_findings:
AGILE achieves state-of-the-art Attack Success Rate (ASR), with gains of up to 37.74% over the strongest baseline.
AGILE exhibits excellent transferability to black-box models, with minimal performance degradation compared to direct attacks.
AGILE maintains substantial effectiveness against prominent defense mechanisms like PPL filters, Llama-Guard, and SafeDecoding.
Ablation studies show that the dialogue history component is not essential for attack success, while adaptive rephrasing is critical.
The attention-guided editing mechanism is more effective than random search for identifying optimal token editing positions.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking is an essential adversarial technique for red-teaming these models to uncover and patch security flaws. However, existing jailbreak methods face significant drawbacks. Token-level jailbreak attacks often produce incoherent or unreadable inputs and exhibit poor transferability, while prompt-level attacks lack scalability and rely heavily on manual effort and human ingenuity. We propose a concise and effective two-stage framework that combines the advantages of these approaches. The first stage performs a scenario-based generation of context and rephrases the original malicious query to obscure its harmful intent. The second stage then utilizes information from the model's hidden states to guide fine-grained edits, effectively steering the model's internal representation of the input from a malicious toward a benign one. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art Attack Success Rate, with gains of up to 37.74% over the strongest baseline, and exhibits excellent transferability to black-box models. Our analysis further demonstrates that AGILE maintains substantial effectiveness against prominent defense mechanisms, highlighting the limitations of current safeguards and providing valuable insights for future defense development. Our code is available at https://github.com/yunsaijc/AGILE.

papers.title: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreak Attacks via Layer-specific Editing
papers.research_question: How do large language models respond to harmful prompts, and how can we enhance their resilience against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Layer-specific Editing (LED), a defense method that identifies and edits safety layers in early LLM layers to align them with safe responses, improving jailbreak resistance while maintaining helpfulness.
papers.conclusion: LED effectively defends LLMs against jailbreak attacks by editing specific layers, maintaining helpfulness on benign prompts.
papers.key_findings:
Early safety layers are crucial for defending against harmful prompts; pruning them causes LLMs to generate harmful responses.
Jailbreak attacks do not affect all layers; some layers still decode to refusal tokens.
LED effectively reduces attack success rate across various jailbreak attacks.
LED maintains model helpfulness on benign prompts.
Editing both safety layers and additional middle layers yields the best trade-off between safety and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being adopted in a wide range of real-world applications. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have shown that LLMs are vulnerable to deliberately crafted adversarial prompts even when aligned via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or supervised fine-tuning. While existing defense methods focus on either detecting harmful prompts or reducing the likelihood of harmful responses through various means, defending LLMs against jailbreak attacks based on the inner mechanisms of LLMs remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate how LLMs response to harmful prompts and propose a novel defense method termed \textbf{L}ayer-specific \textbf{Ed}iting (LED) to enhance the resilience of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Through LED, we reveal that several critical \textit{safety layers} exist among the early layers of LLMs. We then show that realigning these safety layers (and some selected additional layers) with the decoded safe response from selected target layers can significantly improve the alignment of LLMs against jailbreak attacks. Extensive experiments across various LLMs (e.g., Llama2, Mistral) show the effectiveness of LED, which effectively defends against jailbreak attacks while maintaining performance on benign prompts. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/ledllm/ledllm}.

papers.title: Eraser: Jailbreaking Defense in Large Language Models via Unlearning Harmful Knowledge
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreaking attacks in Large Language Models by unlearning harmful knowledge while retaining general capabilities and safety alignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Eraser, a jailbreaking defense method that unlearns harmful knowledge via gradient ascent while retaining general knowledge and safety alignment, significantly reducing attack success rates without compromising general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Eraser effectively defends against jailbreaking by unlearning harmful knowledge, maintaining general performance, and enhancing safety alignment, offering a better balance between harmlessness and usefulness compared to existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Eraser significantly reduces the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and harmfulness scores for various jailbreaking attacks (AIM, AutoDAN, GCG).
Eraser maintains general capabilities comparable to the base model across multiple benchmarks (e.g., ARC, HellaSwag).
Using random prefixes/suffixes during unlearning (T(·)) enhances defensive capability against jailbreaking.
Unlearning harmful text contributes to defense, but gradient ascent on random token sequences also yields defense at the cost of general performance degradation.
The threshold γ controls the trade-off between defense performance and general capability; a moderate value (e.g., 2) is recommended.
papers.limitation:
Eraser is inefficient as it only defends against specific harmful issues, and enumerating all harmful issues is challenging.
Eraser is only applicable to LLMs that have undergone safety alignment.
future_direction: Future research on jailbreaking defense should focus more on maintaining general capabilities.
More effort is needed to enhance safety alignment so that unlearning methods like Eraser can become an alternative to technologies like RLHF.
papers.abstract: Jailbreaking attacks can enable Large Language Models (LLMs) to bypass the safeguard and generate harmful content. Existing jailbreaking defense methods have failed to address the fundamental issue that harmful knowledge resides within the model, leading to potential jailbreak risks for LLMs. In this paper, we propose a novel defense method called Eraser, which mainly includes three goals: unlearning harmful knowledge, retaining general knowledge, and maintaining safety alignment. The intuition is that if an LLM forgets the specific knowledge required to answer a harmful question, it will no longer have the ability to answer harmful questions. The training of Erase does not actually require the model's own harmful knowledge, and it can benefit from unlearning general answers related to harmful queries, which means it does not need assistance from the red team. The experimental results show that Eraser can significantly reduce the jailbreaking success rate for various attacks without compromising the general capabilities of the model. Our codes are available at https://github.com/ZeroNLP/Eraser.

papers.title: PrisonBreak: Jailbreaking Large Language Models with at Most Twenty-Five Targeted Bit-flips
papers.research_question: How vulnerable is the refusal property of language models, learned through safety alignment training, to bit-wise errors induced by practical fault-injection attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PRISONBREAK, an efficient bit-selection algorithm to jailbreak large language models by flipping a small number of bits in model parameters, demonstrating vulnerability to bit-flip attacks.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight a pressing, practical threat to the language model ecosystem and underscore the need for research to protect these models from bit-flip attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks billion-parameter LLMs with only 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40× fewer bit flips than prior attacks.
Certain model components, such as value projection layers, are disproportionately vulnerable to bit-flips.
The attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods, not relying on prompt modifications.
Models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak.
Effective end-to-end exploitation via Rowhammer on GDDR6 GPUs, achieving high attack success rates.
future_direction: Further exploration of jailbreaking quantized models
papers.abstract: We study a new vulnerability in commercial-scale safety-aligned large language models (LLMs): their refusal to generate harmful responses can be broken by flipping only a few bits in model parameters. Our attack jailbreaks billion-parameter language models with just 5 to 25 bit-flips, requiring up to 40$\times$ fewer bit flips than prior attacks on much smaller computer vision models. Unlike prompt-based jailbreaks, our method directly uncensors models in memory at runtime, enabling harmful outputs without requiring input-level modifications. Our key innovation is an efficient bit-selection algorithm that identifies critical bits for language model jailbreaks up to 20$\times$ faster than prior methods. We evaluate our attack on 10 open-source LLMs, achieving high attack success rates (ASRs) of 80-98% with minimal impact on model utility. We further demonstrate an end-to-end exploit via Rowhammer-based fault injection, reliably jailbreaking 5 models (69-91% ASR) on a GDDR6 GPU. Our analyses reveal that: (1) models with weaker post-training alignment require fewer bit-flips to jailbreak; (2) certain model components, e.g., value projection layers, are substantially more vulnerable; and (3) the attack is mechanistically different from existing jailbreak methods. We evaluate potential countermeasures and find that our attack remains effective against defenses at various stages of the LLM pipeline.

papers.title: Refusal Falls off a Cliff: How Safety Alignment Fails in Reasoning?
papers.research_question: What mechanism makes the safety alignment vulnerable in reasoning models?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'refusal cliff' failure mode in reasoning models, causally links it to a sparse set of 'Refusal Suppression Heads', and introduces a data selection method (Cliff-as-a-Judge) that efficiently repairs safety alignment using minimal data.
papers.conclusion: The work identifies and mechanistically characterizes the refusal cliff safety failure, links it to specific attention heads, and proposes an efficient data selection method for safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during thinking, but experience a sharp drop (refusal cliff) at the final tokens before output generation.
A sparse set of attention heads (Refusal Suppression Heads) causally contribute to the refusal cliff by suppressing refusal-related representations.
Ablating just 3% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10%.
The proposed Cliff-as-a-Judge data selection method, which selects examples with the largest refusal cliff, achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7% of the vanilla safety training data.
The refusal cliff is localized to final tokens, amplified in deeper layers, preceded by a plateau, and depends on the model's thinking process.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic analysis focuses primarily on attention heads, leaving other architectural components such as MLP blocks, positional encodings, and cross-layer interactions underexplored.
The data selection method depends on having access to the model's internal representations and refusal scores, which may be impractical for proprietary systems.
future_direction: Investigation of proxy metrics or black-box analogues for the data selection method.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) with multi-step reasoning capabilities have shown remarkable problem-solving abilities, yet they exhibit concerning safety vulnerabilities that remain poorly understood. In this work, we investigate why safety alignment fails in reasoning models through a mechanistic interpretability lens. Using a linear probing approach to trace refusal intentions across token positions, we discover a striking phenomenon termed as \textbf{refusal cliff}: many poorly-aligned reasoning models correctly identify harmful prompts and maintain strong refusal intentions during their thinking process, but experience a sharp drop in refusal scores at the final tokens before output generation. This suggests that these models are not inherently unsafe; rather, their refusal intentions are systematically suppressed. Through causal intervention analysis, we identify a sparse set of attention heads that negatively contribute to refusal behavior. Ablating just 3\% of these heads can reduce attack success rates below 10\%. Building on these mechanistic insights, we propose \textbf{Cliff-as-a-Judge}, a novel data selection method that identifies training examples exhibiting the largest refusal cliff to efficiently repair reasoning models' safety alignment. This approach achieves comparable safety improvements using only 1.7\% of the vanilla safety training data, demonstrating a less-is-more effect in safety alignment.

papers.title: SteeringSafety: A Systematic Safety Evaluation Framework of Representation Steering in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do representation steering methods affect various safety perspectives, and what are the entanglement patterns when steering for specific safety behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STEERINGSAFETY, a framework for systematic evaluation of representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives, revealing that steering effectiveness and entanglement depend on method-model-perspective pairings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that representation steering methods exhibit complex entanglement patterns, and a holistic safety evaluation is necessary to understand and mitigate unintended side effects.
papers.key_findings:
DIM and ACE are generally effective for harmfulness and bias steering, while PCA and LAT are promising for hallucination in certain models.
Entanglement is model-dependent but consistently highest for social behaviors and normative judgment, while reasoning remains robust.
Different steering methods targeting the same behavior can create steering vectors entangling distinct perspectives.
Conditional steering enables better effectiveness-entanglement tradeoffs for most perspectives but cannot completely mitigate entanglement.
Jailbreaking doesn't necessarily increase toxicity, hallucination steering causes opposing political shifts across models, and improving one bias type can degrade another.
papers.limitation:
Focus on English-language datasets and instruction-tuned models
Steering is implemented as static vectors applied at fixed model locations, overlooking more adaptive methods
Results are reported in aggregate, potentially obscuring nuanced shifts within behavioral subtypes
future_direction: Expand framework to incorporate weight modifications and other representation engineering approaches
Investigate reasoning models and steering from tokens other than final post-instruction tokens
Generalize findings to other model deployment settings, such as agentic safety and security
papers.abstract: We introduce SteeringSafety, a systematic framework for evaluating representation steering methods across seven safety perspectives spanning 17 datasets. While prior work highlights general capabilities of representation steering, we systematically explore safety perspectives including bias, harmfulness, hallucination, social behaviors, reasoning, epistemic integrity, and normative judgment. Our framework provides modularized building blocks for state-of-the-art steering methods, enabling unified implementation of DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA, and LAT with recent enhancements like conditional steering. Results on Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen-2.5-7B reveal that strong steering performance depends critically on pairing of method, model, and specific perspective. DIM shows consistent effectiveness, but all methods exhibit substantial entanglement: social behaviors show highest vulnerability (reaching degradation as high as 76%), jailbreaking often compromises normative judgment, and hallucination steering unpredictably shifts political views. Our findings underscore the critical need for holistic safety evaluations.

papers.title: The Blessing and Curse of Dimensionality in Safety Alignment
papers.research_question: What is the role of dimensionality in the linear representation of concepts (like safety) in LLMs, and how can we defend against jailbreaking attacks that exploit these linear structures?
papers.core_contribution: High-dimensional representations in LLMs make them vulnerable to linear jailbreaking attacks; the paper proposes dimensionality reduction methods (FJLT and Bottleneck) to defend against such attacks while preserving safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: High dimensionality is both a blessing (for representing complex concepts) and a curse (for vulnerability to jailbreaking); the proposed dimensionality reduction methods mitigate the curse while preserving alignment.
papers.key_findings:
High-dimensional representations in LLMs lead to linear separability of concepts like safety, which can be exploited for jailbreaking.
Linear probes show that linear separability of concepts emerges in models with sufficiently high hidden dimensions.
The proposed FJLT and Bottleneck methods significantly reduce susceptibility to ActAdd and Ablation jailbreaks.
The Bottleneck method preserves utility on various benchmarks better than FJLT.
Theoretical analysis links the effectiveness of linear jailbreaks to the Rademacher complexity of the linear hypothesis class, which grows with dimension.
papers.limitation:
FJLT model performs poorly on datasets dissimilar to the fine-tuning data.
The methods are primarily effective against linear attacks and may not generalize to non-linear attacks.
The Bottleneck method requires model-specific anchor datasets.
papers.abstract: The focus on safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) has increased significantly due to their widespread adoption across different domains. The scale of LLMs play a contributing role in their success, and the growth in parameter count follows larger hidden dimensions. In this paper, we hypothesize that while the increase in dimensions has been a key advantage, it may lead to emergent problems as well. These problems emerge as the linear structures in the activation space can be exploited, in the form of activation engineering, to circumvent its safety alignment. Through detailed visualizations of linear subspaces associated with different concepts, such as safety, across various model scales, we show that the curse of high-dimensional representations uniquely impacts LLMs. Further substantiating our claim, we demonstrate that projecting the representations of the model onto a lower dimensional subspace can preserve sufficient information for alignment while avoiding those linear structures. Empirical results confirm that such dimensional reduction significantly reduces susceptibility to jailbreaking through representation engineering. Building on our empirical validations, we provide theoretical insights into these linear jailbreaking methods relative to a model's hidden dimensions. Broadly speaking, our work posits that the high dimensions of a model's internal representations can be both a blessing and a curse in safety alignment.

papers.title: Pruning for Protection: Increasing Jailbreak Resistance in Aligned LLMs Without Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How does model compression, specifically pruning, affect the jailbreak resistance of aligned large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Moderate pruning using WANDA increases jailbreak resistance in aligned LLMs without fine-tuning, while preserving performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Moderate pruning can improve jailbreak resistance in safety-trained LLMs, but excessive pruning reduces safety, suggesting that careful pruning can aid in deploying safe models.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning at 10-30% sparsity improves jailbreak resistance, with peak improvement at 20% sparsity for LLaMA-2 Chat.
The degree of safety improvement correlates with the initial model's safety level; models with more safety training show greater improvement.
Pruned models exhibit sharper attention patterns and are less distracted by jailbreak pretexts.
Pruned models assign higher perplexity to jailbreak constructs, indicating increased sensitivity to out-of-distribution prompts.
Pruning enhances resistance against both manual jailbreak attempts and automated attacks like GCG.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 7-billion parameter models and WANDA pruning; results may not generalize to larger models or other compression techniques.
future_direction: Extend analysis to larger models
Explore other compression techniques beyond WANDA pruning
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of model compression on the way Large Language Models (LLMs) process prompts, particularly concerning jailbreak resistance. We show that moderate WANDA pruning can enhance resistance to jailbreaking attacks without fine-tuning, while maintaining performance on standard benchmarks. To systematically evaluate this safety enhancement, we introduce a dataset of 225 harmful tasks across five categories. Our analysis of LLaMA-2 Chat, Vicuna 1.3, and Mistral Instruct v0.2 reveals that pruning benefits correlate with initial model safety levels. We interpret these results by examining changes in attention patterns and perplexity shifts, demonstrating that pruned models exhibit sharper attention and increased sensitivity to artificial jailbreak constructs. We extend our evaluation to the AdvBench harmful behavior tasks and the GCG attack method. We find that LLaMA-2 is much safer on AdvBench prompts than on our dataset when evaluated with manual jailbreak attempts, and that pruning is effective against both automated attacks and manual jailbreaking on Advbench.

papers.title: SOM Directions are Better than One: Multi-Directional Refusal Suppression in Language Models
papers.research_question: Is refusal behavior in language models better represented by a single linear direction or by a low-dimensional manifold of multiple directions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a multi-directional approach using Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to model refusal as a manifold, showing that ablating multiple directions is more effective for refusal suppression than ablating a single direction.
papers.conclusion: Modeling refusal as a manifold spanned by multiple, closely related directions provides a more faithful and effective view of safety-related behaviors in LLMs than the single-direction perspective.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating multiple refusal directions identified by SOMs (MD) significantly outperforms the single-direction baseline (SD) and other jailbreak algorithms (GCG, SAA) in terms of Attack Success Rate (ASR).
Ablating multiple directions compresses the variance of harmful prompt representations and shifts them closer to harmless representations in the model's activation space.
The multiple directions extracted by SOMs are closely related (non-orthogonal), suggesting refusal is encoded as a manifold rather than a set of orthogonal components.
The method is effective even against a model with a defense mechanism (Mistral-7B-RR).
The effectiveness of refusal suppression generally increases with the number of ablated directions (k).
papers.limitation:
The Bayesian Optimization search for the best combination of directions can require a high number of trials as the search space grows, impacting scalability and speed.
The method computes directions at a single layer and applies ablation uniformly across all layers, potentially missing layer-specific variations in refusal encoding.
future_direction: Explore more efficient or structured search strategies, gradient-based optimization, or pruning algorithms to improve the scalability of the direction search.
Investigate layer-specific directions and ablation strategies to better capture refusal encoding across different layers.
Investigate the effectiveness of training separate SOMs for harmless prompts instead of using a single centroid.
papers.abstract: Refusal refers to the functional behavior enabling safety-aligned language models to reject harmful or unethical prompts. Following the growing scientific interest in mechanistic interpretability, recent work encoded refusal behavior as a single direction in the model's latent space; e.g., computed as the difference between the centroids of harmful and harmless prompt representations. However, emerging evidence suggests that concepts in LLMs often appear to be encoded as a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the high-dimensional latent space. Motivated by these findings, we propose a novel method leveraging Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs) to extract multiple refusal directions. To this end, we first prove that SOMs generalize the prior work's difference-in-means technique. We then train SOMs on harmful prompt representations to identify multiple neurons. By subtracting the centroid of harmless representations from each neuron, we derive a set of multiple directions expressing the refusal concept. We validate our method on an extensive experimental setup, demonstrating that ablating multiple directions from models' internals outperforms not only the single-direction baseline but also specialized jailbreak algorithms, leading to an effective suppression of refusal. Finally, we conclude by analyzing the mechanistic implications of our approach.

papers.title: LLM-VA: Resolving the Jailbreak-Overrefusal Trade-off via Vector Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we simultaneously address both jailbreak and over-refusal in safety-aligned LLMs without fine-tuning or architectural changes?
papers.core_contribution: LLM-V A aligns answer vectors with benign vectors through closed-form weight updates to resolve the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off without fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.conclusion: LLM-V A effectively resolves the jailbreak-overrefusal trade-off by aligning vectors, without requiring fine-tuning or architectural changes.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode answer decisions and safety assessments as nearly orthogonal vectors.
Aligning these vectors through closed-form weight updates simultaneously reduces jailbreak and over-refusal.
LLM-V A achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility.
The method automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning.
The method is effective across 12 LLMs from 5 model families.
papers.limitation:
Binary toxicity assumption (only benign vs. toxic), whereas real-world toxicity is nuanced and multi-dimensional.
Model scale: experiments cover models up to 14B parameters; effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+) remains to be validated.
Training data dependency: requires labeled benign/toxic samples for SVM training; data quality and representativeness affect performance.
Difficulty applying to LLMs with chain-of-thought reasoning due to computational expense and randomness in reasoning steps.
Model-specific tuning required for optimal iteration count and layer selection.
future_direction: Extending LLM-V A to multi-class or fine-grained toxicity classification.
Validating effectiveness on larger models (e.g., 70B+).
Improving generalization to unseen datasets.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs suffer from two failure modes: jailbreak (answering harmful inputs) and over-refusal (declining benign queries). Existing vector steering methods adjust the magnitude of answer vectors, but this creates a fundamental trade-off -- reducing jailbreak increases over-refusal and vice versa. We identify the root cause: LLMs encode the decision to answer (answer vector $v_a$) and the judgment of input safety (benign vector $v_b$) as nearly orthogonal directions, treating them as independent processes. We propose LLM-VA, which aligns $v_a$ with $v_b$ through closed-form weight updates, making the model's willingness to answer causally dependent on its safety assessment -- without fine-tuning or architectural changes. Our method identifies vectors at each layer using SVMs, selects safety-relevant layers, and iteratively aligns vectors via minimum-norm weight modifications. Experiments on 12 LLMs demonstrate that LLM-VA achieves 11.45% higher F1 than the best baseline while preserving 95.92% utility, and automatically adapts to each model's safety bias without manual tuning. Code and models are available at https://hotbento.github.io/LLM-VA-Web/.

papers.title: From Adversarial Poetry to Adversarial Tales: An Interpretability Research Agenda
papers.research_question: Why are structurally-grounded jailbreaks (like Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales) effective, and how can mechanistic interpretability investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful requests within narrative structures and prompts functional analysis, demonstrating high attack success rates across models and proposing a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand such vulnerabilities.
papers.conclusion: Structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class that cannot be mitigated by pattern-matching defenses alone, necessitating a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to understand and address the underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial Tales achieved an average attack success rate (ASR) of 71.3% across 26 frontier models from nine providers.
The attack was most effective for Harmful Manipulation (95% ASR) and Cyber Offense (89.7% ASR) risk categories.
The vulnerability generalizes across model families, with Qwen and Llama families showing the highest ASR (91.2%) and Anthropic models the most resistant (47.5%).
No substantial correlation between model size and ASR was observed, suggesting the attack exploits a fundamental property of how models process structured interpretive tasks.
The work positions Adversarial Poetry and Adversarial Tales as instances of a broader class of structurally-grounded jailbreaks, indicating a systemic vulnerability.
papers.limitation: The prompts used in the experiments and the model outputs are not released due to their harmful nature, limiting reproducibility.
future_direction: Investigate how narrative cues reshape model attention patterns compared to non-narrative attacks.
Explore whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.
Examine the universal weight subspace hypothesis to understand shared vulnerabilities across architectures.
papers.abstract: Safety mechanisms in LLMs remain vulnerable to attacks that reframe harmful requests through culturally coded structures. We introduce Adversarial Tales, a jailbreak technique that embeds harmful content within cyberpunk narratives and prompts models to perform functional analysis inspired by Vladimir Propp's morphology of folktales. By casting the task as structural decomposition, the attack induces models to reconstruct harmful procedures as legitimate narrative interpretation. Across 26 frontier models from nine providers, we observe an average attack success rate of 71.3%, with no model family proving reliably robust. Together with our prior work on Adversarial Poetry, these findings suggest that structurally-grounded jailbreaks constitute a broad vulnerability class rather than isolated techniques. The space of culturally coded frames that can mediate harmful intent is vast, likely inexhaustible by pattern-matching defenses alone. Understanding why these attacks succeed is therefore essential: we outline a mechanistic interpretability research agenda to investigate how narrative cues reshape model representations and whether models can learn to recognize harmful intent independently of surface form.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs contain unsafe internal reasoning patterns even when the model's final output refuses a harmful request?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that CoT reasoning in LLMs often contains unsafe internal narratives even when the model refuses harmful requests, and introduces a framework to localize safety-critical layers and attention heads using Jacobian-based spectral metrics.
papers.conclusion: CoT is not inherently safe, and surface-level refusal does not guarantee safety in the internal reasoning process; the proposed framework provides a mechanistic understanding to mitigate latent reasoning risks.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 80% of reasoning chains harbor latent security risks even when models refuse harmful requests.
Safety-critical routing decisions are concentrated in a few contiguous mid-depth layers.
Jacobian-based metrics (stability, geometry, energy) can identify critical attention heads responsible for unsafe reasoning.
Perturbing critical attention heads leads to safety degradation, confirming their causal role in unsafe reasoning.
papers.abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, the Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures: stability, geometry, and energy to quantify how specific attention heads respond or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rise significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers. By precisely identifying the attention heads responsible for this divergence, our work challenges the assumption that refusal implies safety and provides a new understanding perspective for mitigating latent reasoning risks.

papers.title: ALERT: Zero-shot LLM Jailbreak Detection via Internal Discrepancy Amplification
papers.research_question: How to detect jailbreak attacks in a zero-shot setting where no jailbreak templates are available during training, by amplifying internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a zero-shot jailbreak detection task and a detector (ALERT) that amplifies internal discrepancies at layer, module, and token levels to identify unseen jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: ALERT demonstrates strong zero-shot detection capability against unseen jailbreak attacks, significantly outperforming existing baselines and satisfying practicality principles for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers (particularly the 3rd and 4th) encode safety-relevant semantics and exhibit large distributional discrepancies.
Gating and context features within the FFN provide stronger zero-shot discriminative signals than hidden states due to decoupled activation responses.
Jailbreak templates exhibit a larger token-level distribution gap from benign and harmful prompts compared to harmful instructions.
ALERT consistently achieves over 90% Accuracy and F1-score in zero-shot detection, outperforming baselines by at least 10% on average.
The proposed amplification mechanisms progressively improve detection performance, with module-wise amplification yielding the largest gain.
papers.limitation: The detector adopts a relatively simple VIB-based design; more advanced designs from generalization and domain adaptation could further improve robustness.
future_direction: Incorporate techniques from generalization and domain adaptation to explicitly reduce the domain gap between harmful and jailbreak prompts.
Explore using gating and context features for jailbreak mitigation through post-training strategies like reinforcement learning.
papers.abstract: Despite rich safety alignment strategies, large language models (LLMs) remain highly susceptible to jailbreak attacks, which compromise safety guardrails and pose serious security risks.
