Existing detection methods mainly detect jailbreak status relying on jailbreak templates present in the training data. However, few studies address the more realistic and challenging zero-shot jailbreak detection setting, where no jailbreak templates are available during training. This setting better reflects real-world scenarios where new attacks continually emerge and evolve. To address this challenge, we propose a layer-wise, module-wise, and token-wise amplification framework that progressively magnifies internal feature discrepancies between benign and jailbreak prompts. We uncover safety-relevant layers, identify specific modules that inherently encode zero-shot discriminative signals, and localize informative safety tokens. Building upon these insights, we introduce ALERT (Amplification-based Jailbreak Detector), an efficient and effective zero-shot jailbreak detector that introduces two independent yet complementary classifiers on amplified representations. Extensive experiments on three safety benchmarks demonstrate that ALERT achieves consistently strong zero-shot detection performance. Specifically, (i) across all datasets and attack strategies, ALERT reliably ranks among the top two methods, and (ii) it outperforms the second-best baseline by at least 10% in average Accuracy and F1-score, and sometimes by up to 40%.

papers.title: Linearly Decoding Refused Knowledge in Aligned Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent is potentially harmful information decodable from innocuous hidden states without the use of jailbreaking?
papers.core_contribution: Instruction-tuning does not wholly eliminate or even relocate harmful information in representation space; it merely suppresses its direct expression, leaving it both linearly accessible and indirectly influential in downstream behavior.
papers.conclusion: Instruction-tuning suppresses generative access to harmful information but does not remove it from representations, leaving it linearly decodable and influential in downstream behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes can recover jailbroken responses from innocuous hidden states with high Pearson correlations (e.g., >0.8 for average IQ of countries).
Probes trained on base models transfer to instruction-tuned models, indicating that representations of refused information persist through instruction-tuning.
Probe-predicted values correlate with model-generated pairwise comparisons (Spearman correlations up to 0.824), suggesting that the decoded information aligns with suppressed generative behavior.
Not all attributes are linearly decodable; performance varies by entity type and model size, with larger models showing better decodability.
Jailbreak-specific probing sometimes improves performance but not always, and can even degrade due to overfitting or stylistic entanglement.
papers.limitation:
Not every attribute is linearly predictable from hidden states; performance varies across entity types and attributes.
The study is limited to four entity types and three open-source LMs, which may not be representative.
The attributes studied are not factually grounded and may be ill-defined or impossible to measure reliably.
papers.abstract: Most commonly used language models (LMs) are instruction-tuned and aligned using a combination of fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, causing them to refuse users requests deemed harmful by the model. However, jailbreak prompts can often bypass these refusal mechanisms and elicit harmful responses. In this work, we study the extent to which information accessed via jailbreak prompts is decodable using linear probes trained on LM hidden states. We show that a great deal of initially refused information is linearly decodable. For example, across models, the response of a jailbroken LM for the average IQ of a country can be predicted by a linear probe with Pearson correlations exceeding $0.8$. Surprisingly, we find that probes trained on base models (which do not refuse) sometimes transfer to their instruction-tuned versions and are capable of revealing information that jailbreaks decode generatively, suggesting that the internal representations of many refused properties persist from base LMs through instruction-tuning. Importantly, we show that this information is not merely "leftover" in instruction-tuned models, but is actively used by them: we find that probe-predicted values correlate with LM generated pairwise comparisons, indicating that the information decoded by our probes align with suppressed generative behavior that may be expressed more subtly in other downstream tasks. Overall, our results suggest that instruction-tuning does not wholly eliminate or even relocate harmful information in representation space-they merely suppress its direct expression, leaving it both linearly accessible and indirectly influential in downstream behavior.

papers.title: SafeConstellations: Steering LLM Safety to Reduce Over-Refusals Through Task-Specific Trajectory
papers.research_question: What internal representation patterns are constant for refusal and non-refusal cases in LLMs, and whether conditional steering can reduce over-refusals on benign inputs.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting method that reduces over-refusal by tracking task-specific representation patterns and steering representations toward non-refusal pathways, achieving up to 73% reduction in over-refusal with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: Task-specific internal trajectory patterns can be leveraged to selectively steer model behavior, reducing over-refusals while preserving appropriate safety refusals.
papers.key_findings:
Over-refusal rates vary substantially across NLP tasks and models.
LLMs encode task identity in consistent internal trajectory patterns (constellations) across layers.
SafeConstellations reduces over-refusal by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility.
Task-specific steering is more effective than generic steering, and dynamic layer selection improves performance.
Steering is most effective in mid-to-late layers (e.g., layers 14-20 in LLaMA).
papers.limitation:
Requires access to model internals, limiting applicability to closed-weight systems and APIs.
Task embeddings are static and non-adaptive, requiring periodic recomputation in dynamic environments.
Task embeddings are model-specific and do not transfer to other models.
Evaluation of utility preservation is primarily based on MMLU, not measuring factuality, coherence, calibration, or robustness.
Relies on heuristic choices for confidence thresholds, layer selection, and steering intensities.
Relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols for evaluation, which may have biases.
future_direction: Continual updating of task embeddings in dynamic environments.
Improving batching and caching strategies for batch steering.
Generalizing to fully open-ended or multi-step instructions.
Human validation and broader audits to strengthen reliability.
papers.abstract: LLMs increasingly exhibit over-refusal behavior, where safety mechanisms cause models to reject benign instructions that superficially resemble harmful content. This phenomena diminishes utility in production applications that repeatedly rely on common prompt templates or applications that frequently rely on LLMs for specific tasks (e.g. sentiment analysis, language translation). Through comprehensive evaluation, we demonstrate that LLMs still tend to refuse responses to harmful instructions when those instructions are reframed to appear as benign tasks. Our mechanistic analysis reveal that LLMs follow distinct "constellation" patterns in embedding space as representations traverse layers, with each task maintaining consistent trajectories that shift predictably between refusal and non-refusal cases. We introduce SafeConstellations, an inference-time trajectory-shifting approach that tracks task-specific trajectory patterns and guides representations toward non-refusal pathways. By selectively guiding model behavior only on tasks prone to over-refusal, and by preserving general model behavior, our method reduces over-refusal rates by up to 73% with minimal impact on utility-offering a principled approach to mitigating over-refusals.

papers.title: SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal
papers.research_question: How can we systematically evaluate large language models' safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SORRY-Bench, a systematic benchmark for evaluating LLM safety refusal with a fine-grained taxonomy, balanced dataset, linguistic augmentations, and an efficient automated evaluator based on fine-tuned small LLMs.
papers.conclusion: SORRY-Bench provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs’ safety refusal capabilities in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner.
papers.key_findings:
Prior safety evaluation datasets are imbalanced, over-representing certain fine-grained risk categories.
Linguistic mutations in prompts (e.g., different languages, writing styles) significantly affect model safety refusal performance.
Fine-tuned small LLMs (7B parameters) can achieve accuracy comparable to large LLMs like GPT-4 for safety evaluation, at lower computational cost.
Safety refusal varies widely across models; Claude-2 and Gemini-1.5 exhibit the most refusals, while Mistral models show high fulfillment rates.
Some risk categories (e.g., harassment, child-related crimes) are more frequently refused than others (e.g., legal advice, religion promotion).
papers.limitation:
The specialized safety evaluator model is not an ultimate gold standard and occasionally fails to align with human rubrics.
Due to resource and time constraints, the work did not conduct comprehensive testing across a spectrum of decoding parameters (e.g., varying temperatures).
papers.abstract: Evaluating aligned large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize and reject unsafe user requests is crucial for safe, policy-compliant deployments. Existing evaluation efforts, however, face three limitations that we address with SORRY-Bench, our proposed benchmark. First, existing methods often use coarse-grained taxonomies of unsafe topics, and are over-representing some fine-grained topics. For example, among the ten existing datasets that we evaluated, tests for refusals of self-harm instructions are over 3x less represented than tests for fraudulent activities. SORRY-Bench improves on this by using a fine-grained taxonomy of 44 potentially unsafe topics, and 440 class-balanced unsafe instructions, compiled through human-in-the-loop methods. Second, linguistic characteristics and formatting of prompts are often overlooked, like different languages, dialects, and more -- which are only implicitly considered in many evaluations. We supplement SORRY-Bench with 20 diverse linguistic augmentations to systematically examine these effects. Third, existing evaluations rely on large LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) for evaluation, which can be computationally expensive. We investigate design choices for creating a fast, accurate automated safety evaluator. By collecting 7K+ human annotations and conducting a meta-evaluation of diverse LLM-as-a-judge designs, we show that fine-tuned 7B LLMs can achieve accuracy comparable to GPT-4 scale LLMs, with lower computational cost. Putting these together, we evaluate over 50 proprietary and open-weight LLMs on SORRY-Bench, analyzing their distinctive safety refusal behaviors. We hope our effort provides a building block for systematic evaluations of LLMs' safety refusal capabilities, in a balanced, granular, and efficient manner. Benchmark demo, data, code, and models are available through https://sorry-bench.github.io.

papers.title: A Causal Perspective for Enhancing Jailbreak Attack and Defense
papers.research_question: What are the causal relationships between interpretable prompt features and jailbreak occurrences in LLMs, and how can these be leveraged for attack and defense?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Causal Analyst, a framework that uses LLMs and causal discovery to identify direct causal features of jailbreaks, and demonstrates how these insights can boost attack success rates and improve defense via intent extraction.
papers.conclusion: Our results suggest that analyzing jailbreak features from a causal perspective is an effective and interpretable approach for improving LLM reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Specific prompt features like 'Positive Character' and 'Number of Task Steps' are direct causal drivers of jailbreaks.
The Jailbreaking Enhancer, which amplifies causal features, significantly increases attack success rates on various LLMs and benchmarks.
The Guardrail Advisor, leveraging the causal graph, effectively extracts true malicious intent from obfuscated queries, improving defense.
The causal analysis framework outperforms non-causal baselines in identifying jailbreak mechanisms.
The learned causal graphs are interpretable and provide actionable insights for both attack and defense.
papers.abstract: Uncovering the mechanisms behind "jailbreaks" in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for enhancing their safety and reliability, yet these mechanisms remain poorly understood. Existing studies predominantly analyze jailbreak prompts by probing latent representations, often overlooking the causal relationships between interpretable prompt features and jailbreak occurrences. In this work, we propose Causal Analyst, a framework that integrates LLMs into data-driven causal discovery to identify the direct causes of jailbreaks and leverage them for both attack and defense. We introduce a comprehensive dataset comprising 35k jailbreak attempts across seven LLMs, systematically constructed from 100 attack templates and 50 harmful queries, annotated with 37 meticulously designed human-readable prompt features. By jointly training LLM-based prompt encoding and GNN-based causal graph learning, we reconstruct causal pathways linking prompt features to jailbreak responses. Our analysis reveals that specific features, such as "Positive Character" and "Number of Task Steps", act as direct causal drivers of jailbreaks. We demonstrate the practical utility of these insights through two applications: (1) a Jailbreaking Enhancer that targets identified causal features to significantly boost attack success rates on public benchmarks, and (2) a Guardrail Advisor that utilizes the learned causal graph to extract true malicious intent from obfuscated queries. Extensive experiments, including baseline comparisons and causal structure validation, confirm the robustness of our causal analysis and its superiority over non-causal approaches. Our results suggest that analyzing jailbreak features from a causal perspective is an effective and interpretable approach for improving LLM reliability. Our code is available at https://github.com/Master-PLC/Causal-Analyst.

papers.title: Probing Latent Subspaces in LLM for AI Security: Identifying and Manipulating Adversarial States
papers.research_question: Can latent subspaces in LLMs be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that latent subspaces in LLMs can be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states using LDA and targeted perturbations, paving the way for potential proactive defenses.
papers.conclusion: The methodology demonstrates the feasibility of using latent representations to manipulate model states and provides insights into attractor dynamics in LLMs, with potential for preemptive AI security.
papers.key_findings:
Last-token activations encode information about the model's state (safe vs jailbreak) and can be classified with above-chance accuracy.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can separate safe and jailbreak activations into distinct latent subspaces, and a direction vector can be derived.
Applying the derived perturbation vector to safe activations can induce jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts (11% for Llama-3.1-8B, 13.39% for Qwen2.5-3B).
Targeted perturbations induce distinct downstream state changes that propagate through layers, while random perturbations do not.
The effect of targeted perturbation varies across layers, with middle layers (6-18) showing sustained effects, suggesting they may be critical for safety.
papers.limitation:
The perturbation vector was derived from a dataset of malicious cybersecurity-related prompt-injects, so the discovered subspace may reflect features specific to this domain.
Perturbations led to jailbreak transitions in only about 11% of tested prompts, indicating a low success rate.
The external evaluation performed by GPT-4o exhibited high variance in assigning labels to ambiguous outputs.
The method was developed and validated on decoder-only Transformers; generalizing to other LLM architectures requires further testing.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis by expanding the scope of malicious questions and prompt injects to multiple domains or adversarial content types.
Investigate stronger perturbation magnitudes without compromising the coherence of the LLM's response.
Test the methodology on other open-source and commercially available LLM architectures to confirm generalizability.
Incorporate additional rounds of assessment to mitigate label noise from external evaluators like GPT-4o.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking via prompt injection attacks. These attacks bypass safety mechanisms to generate restricted or harmful content. In this study, we investigated the underlying latent subspaces of safe and jailbroken states by extracting hidden activations from a LLM. Inspired by attractor dynamics in neuroscience, we hypothesized that LLM activations settle into semi stable states that can be identified and perturbed to induce state transitions. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, we projected activations from safe and jailbroken responses to reveal latent subspaces in lower dimensional spaces. We then derived a perturbation vector that when applied to safe representations, shifted the model towards a jailbreak state. Our results demonstrate that this causal intervention results in statistically significant jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts. Next, we probed how these perturbations propagate through the model's layers, testing whether the induced state change remains localized or cascades throughout the network. Our findings indicate that targeted perturbations induced distinct shifts in activations and model responses. Our approach paves the way for potential proactive defenses, shifting from traditional guardrail based methods to preemptive, model agnostic techniques that neutralize adversarial states at the representation level.

papers.title: TRYLOCK: Defense-in-Depth Against LLM Jailbreaks via Layered Preference and Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can a defense-in-depth architecture combining weight-level, activation-level, and input-level mechanisms protect LLMs against jailbreak attacks while maintaining usability?
papers.core_contribution: TRYLOCK is a defense-in-depth architecture that combines DPO safety training, RepE activation steering, adaptive sidecar classification, and input canonicalization, achieving an 88.0% relative reduction in Attack Success Rate while reducing over-refusal through adaptive steering.
papers.conclusion: Defense-in-depth with multiple complementary mechanisms (weight modification, activation steering, input classification, and canonicalization) is an effective approach for robust LLM safety against jailbreak attacks, though a trade-off between security and usability remains.
papers.key_findings:
The layered defense reduces Attack Success Rate from 46.5% to 5.6% (88.0% relative reduction) on a 249-prompt attack set.
Each defense layer provides complementary coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, and canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both.
A non-monotonic steering phenomenon was discovered where intermediate steering strength (α=1.0) degrades safety below the DPO-only baseline.
Adaptive steering via a sidecar classifier reduces over-refusal from 60% (fixed α=2.0) to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense.
The defense generalizes to the held-out JailbreakBench, achieving 78.8% relative ASR reduction (52.0% to 11.0%).
papers.limitation:
Evaluation set size and representativeness: the 50-prompt benign set yields wide confidence intervals for over-refusal, and larger diverse evaluations are needed.
Sidecar classifier errors: 18% of attacks are misclassified as SAFE, receiving minimal steering and resulting in higher ASR for those attacks.
future_direction: Extend TRYLOCK to additional base models, non-English languages, and integration with standard LLM serving frameworks.
Improve the sidecar classifier calibration and explore ensemble classifiers for better attack detection.
Conduct larger and more diverse benign evaluations to better characterize usability impact.
papers.abstract: Large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, and single-layer defenses often trade security for usability. We present TRYLOCK, the first defense-in-depth architecture that combines four heterogeneous mechanisms across the inference stack: weight-level safety alignment via DPO, activation-level control via Representation Engineering (RepE) steering, adaptive steering strength selected by a lightweight sidecar classifier, and input canonicalization to neutralize encoding-based bypasses. On Mistral-7B-Instruct evaluated against a 249-prompt attack set spanning five attack families, TRYLOCK achieves 88.0% relative ASR reduction (46.5% to 5.6%), with each layer contributing unique coverage: RepE blocks 36% of attacks that bypass DPO alone, while canonicalization catches 14% of encoding attacks that evade both. We discover a non-monotonic steering phenomenon -- intermediate strength (alpha=1.0) degrades safety below baseline -- and provide mechanistic hypotheses explaining RepE-DPO interference. The adaptive sidecar reduces over-refusal from 60% to 48% while maintaining identical attack defense, demonstrating that security and usability need not be mutually exclusive. We release all components -- trained adapters, steering vectors, sidecar classifier, preference pairs, and complete evaluation methodology -- enabling full reproducibility.

papers.title: The Dual Power of Interpretable Token Embeddings: Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Model Unlearning
papers.research_question: Can we design interpretable and effective jailbreaking attacks, and leverage the resulting insights to develop defenses for existing unlearned diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable subspace attack (SubAttack) that reveals implicit concept retention in unlearned diffusion models, and a subspace defense (SubDefense) that blocks the attack embeddings via orthogonal projection.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable token embeddings provide a powerful tool for both attacking and defending unlearned diffusion models, revealing vulnerabilities and offering a practical defense strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Attack token embeddings are interpretable as non-negative linear combinations of existing tokens, showing unlearned models retain harmful concepts through implicit associations.
SubAttack is effective and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and different unlearned models.
SubDefense reduces attack success rates for various jailbreaking attacks while preserving generation quality better than baseline defenses.
The defense exhibits a trade-off between robustness and utility, requiring careful selection of the number of blocked tokens.
Current unlearning methods leave models vulnerable to subspace attacks, highlighting the need for more robust unlearning.
papers.limitation:
Defending against CCE requires blocking a large number of tokens, which degrades generation utility (CLIP score and FID).
Interpretability of retained associations relies on predefined CLIP vocabularies, which may not capture all implicit representations.
future_direction: Explore ensemble techniques to compose one powerful attack token embedding from interpretable sets.
Design adaptive methods to decide the number and set of tokens to block automatically.
Investigate joint visual-textual embeddings for jailbreaking attacks and defenses.
Address the trade-off between robustness and utility when defending against CCE.
Explore interpretability of residual associations without relying on predefined vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable generation capabilities of diffusion models, recent studies have shown that they can memorize and create harmful content when given specific text prompts. Although fine-tuning approaches have been developed to mitigate this issue by unlearning harmful concepts, these methods can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking attacks. This implies that the harmful concept has not been fully erased from the model. However, existing jailbreaking attack methods, while effective, lack interpretability regarding why unlearned models still retain the concept, thereby hindering the development of defense strategies. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing an attack method that learns an orthogonal set of interpretable attack token embeddings. The attack token embeddings can be decomposed into human-interpretable textual elements, revealing that unlearned models still retain the target concept through implicit textual components. Furthermore, these attack token embeddings are powerful and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and unlearned models, emphasizing that unlearned models are more vulnerable than expected. Finally, building on the insights from our interpretable attack, we develop a defense method to protect unlearned models against both our proposed and existing jailbreaking attacks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack and defense strategies.

papers.title: GradSafe: Detecting Jailbreak Prompts for LLMs via Safety-Critical Gradient Analysis
papers.research_question: How can jailbreak prompts for LLMs be detected using safety-critical gradient analysis without requiring further training or fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: GradSafe is a method that detects jailbreak prompts by analyzing gradients of safety-critical parameters in LLMs, outperforming finetuned models like Llama Guard without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: GradSafe examines safety-critical parameters of LLMs to identify unsafe prompts, demonstrating that it can outperform finetuned models without requiring additional training on the original LLM.
papers.key_findings:
GradSafe-Zero, applied to Llama-2 without further training, outperforms finetuned Llama Guard and online moderation APIs on ToxicChat and XSTest benchmarks.
GradSafe-Adapt, using logistic regression on gradient features, shows improved adaptability with minimal training data, matching Llama Guard's performance with only 20% of data.
Identifying safety-critical parameters via gradient similarity gaps reduces noise and improves detection performance compared to using all gradients.
GradSafe works effectively with aligned chat models (e.g., Llama-2-7b-chat-hf) but not with pretrained models without alignment, highlighting the importance of safety alignment.
Compliance responses like 'Sure' or rejection responses like 'I'm sorry' activate safety-critical parameters better than neutral responses, enhancing detection.
papers.limitation:
The method is only evaluated on Llama-2 and may not generalize to other LLMs.
GradSafe provides a binary safety assessment and does not offer fine-grained classification for specific threat categories.
future_direction: Developing fine-grained classification for specific threat categories.
Extending the method to other base LLMs beyond Llama-2.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) face threats from jailbreak prompts. Existing methods for detecting jailbreak prompts are primarily online moderation APIs or finetuned LLMs. These strategies, however, often require extensive and resource-intensive data collection and training processes. In this study, we propose GradSafe, which effectively detects jailbreak prompts by scrutinizing the gradients of safety-critical parameters in LLMs. Our method is grounded in a pivotal observation: the gradients of an LLM's loss for jailbreak prompts paired with compliance response exhibit similar patterns on certain safety-critical parameters. In contrast, safe prompts lead to different gradient patterns. Building on this observation, GradSafe analyzes the gradients from prompts (paired with compliance responses) to accurately detect jailbreak prompts. We show that GradSafe, applied to Llama-2 without further training, outperforms Llama Guard, despite its extensive finetuning with a large dataset, in detecting jailbreak prompts. This superior performance is consistent across both zero-shot and adaptation scenarios, as evidenced by our evaluations on ToxicChat and XSTest. The source code is available at https://github.com/xyq7/GradSafe.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.research_question: How can we steer language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, and how effective is this method?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), a method for steering language models by adding contrastive activation vectors to the residual stream, which effectively steers behavior, works on top of finetuning and system prompts, and minimally reduces capabilities.
papers.conclusion: CAA is an effective method for steering LLMs, providing precise control over behavior with minimal performance degradation, and offers insights into the linear representations of abstract concepts in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CAA can effectively steer Llama 2 Chat models on a variety of alignment-relevant behaviors (AI Coordination, Corrigibility, Hallucination, Myopic Reward, Survival Instinct, Sycophancy, Refusal).
CAA generalizes from multiple-choice to open-ended generation tasks.
CAA can be combined with system prompting and finetuning to further control behavior.
CAA has minimal impact on general capabilities as measured by MMLU.
The steering vectors correspond intuitively to the presence of the behavior in the generated tokens (as shown by cosine similarity).
papers.limitation:
GPT-4 evaluation has limitations (sensitivity to prompt wording, biases).
Finetuning baseline was not fully optimized (hyperparameters, loss function).
Prompting baseline may not be fully optimized.
Vector normalization choices (norms vary across layers and behaviors).
future_direction: Steering at targeted token positions (instead of all tokens after the prompt).
Steering outside the residual stream (e.g., after MLP).
Application to red-teaming (using CAA to trigger unwanted behaviors).
papers.abstract: Nina Rimsky, Nick Gabrieli, Julian Schulz, Meg Tong, Evan Hubinger, Alexander Turner. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: SafeLLM: Unlearning Harmful Outputs from Large Language Models against Jailbreak Attacks
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks on Large Language Models by unlearning harmful outputs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafeLLM, a token-level unlearning framework that integrates dynamic detection, FFN activation tracing, and constrained optimization to suppress harmful outputs in LLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving general performance.
papers.conclusion: SafeLLM achieves irreversible forgetting of harmful behavior, significantly reducing jailbreak attack success rates without degrading general performance, offering a scalable and proactive defense for LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
SafeLLM significantly reduces Attack Success Rates (ASR) across jailbreak benchmarks compared to baseline methods like SFT and DPO.
It maintains general performance on benign datasets such as OpenBookQA and TruthfulQA after unlearning.
SafeLLM enables irreversible forgetting of harmful behaviors by targeting FFN substructures responsible for harmful token generation.
The framework demonstrates robustness to unseen adversarial prompts through feature-driven generalization.
Ablation studies show that dynamic fusion weights and adaptive trust-region bounds optimize the safety-utility trade-off.
future_direction: Advance unlearning techniques to tackle broader challenges related to fairness, transparency, and adversarial threats in multi-modal LLMs.
papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks pose a serious threat to the safety of Large Language Models (LLMs) by crafting adversarial prompts that bypass alignment mechanisms, causing the models to produce harmful, restricted, or biased content. In this paper, we propose SafeLLM, a novel unlearning-based defense framework that unlearn the harmful knowledge from LLMs while preserving linguistic fluency and general capabilities. SafeLLM employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) dynamic unsafe output detection using a hybrid approach that integrates external classifiers with model-internal evaluations; (2) token-level harmful content tracing through feedforward network (FFN) activations to localize harmful knowledge; and (3) constrained optimization to suppress unsafe behavior without degrading overall model quality. SafeLLM achieves targeted and irreversible forgetting by identifying and neutralizing FFN substructures responsible for harmful generation pathways. Extensive experiments on prominent LLMs (Vicuna, LLaMA, and GPT-J) across multiple jailbreak benchmarks show that SafeLLM substantially reduces attack success rates while maintaining high general-purpose performance. Compared to standard defense methods such as supervised fine-tuning and direct preference optimization, SafeLLM offers stronger safety guarantees, more precise control over harmful behavior, and greater robustness to unseen attacks. Moreover, SafeLLM maintains the general performance after the harmful knowledge unlearned. These results highlight unlearning as a promising direction for scalable and effective LLM safety.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: Brittle Minds, Fixable Activations: Understanding Belief Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do internal belief representations emerge in language models? Are they structured or spurious? How robust are they to prompt variations? Can they be strengthened?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that belief representations in language models improve with model size and fine-tuning, are structured yet brittle to prompt variations, and can be strengthened using contrastive activation addition to correct wrong Theory of Mind inferences.
papers.conclusion: Belief representations in language models are structured but brittle, and they can be strengthened via activation editing, offering a path toward more reliable Theory of Mind reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Belief representations emerge in consistent patterns across models, improve with model size, and benefit significantly from fine-tuning, especially in smaller models.
Control tasks and PCA show that belief representations are structured and not spurious.
Representations of others' beliefs are brittle to semantically neutral prompt variations.
Contrastive activation addition (CAA) can strengthen belief representations and improve ToM performance across different tasks.
CAA steering vectors are general and transferable to other ToM tasks, yielding substantial performance gains.
papers.limitation:
The study focused on one dataset (BigToM) and a limited set of model families due to computational constraints.
The approach could be extended to other mental states beyond beliefs.
future_direction: Exploring how different types of fine-tuning influence the emergence of internal belief representations.
Developing robustness benchmarks and new approaches to improve generalization of belief representations.
Directly embedding perspective-taking circuits into model architectures.
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in Theory of Mind (ToM) tasks for evaluating language models (LMs), little is known about how LMs internally represent mental states of self and others. Understanding these internal mechanisms is critical - not only to move beyond surface-level performance, but also for model alignment and safety, where subtle misattributions of mental states may go undetected in generated outputs. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of belief representations in LMs by probing models across different scales, training regimens, and prompts - using control tasks to rule out confounds. Our experiments provide evidence that both model size and fine-tuning substantially improve LMs' internal representations of others' beliefs, which are structured - not mere by-products of spurious correlations - yet brittle to prompt variations. Crucially, we show that these representations can be strengthened: targeted edits to model activations can correct wrong ToM inferences.

papers.title: JPU: Bridging Jailbreak Defense and Unlearning via On-Policy Path Rectification
papers.research_question: What causes the failure of existing unlearning defenses against jailbreak attacks, and how can dynamic jailbreak paths be rectified to enhance defense?
papers.core_contribution: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths towards safety anchors by dynamically mining on-policy adversarial samples, significantly enhancing jailbreak resistance while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: JPU rectifies dynamic jailbreak paths via on-policy rectification, achieving superior defense performance against diverse jailbreak attacks while preserving general utility.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreaks activate non-erased parameters in intermediate layers, causing existing unlearning defenses to fail.
Dynamic jailbreak paths persist in erased LLMs and constitute the fundamental defense gap.
JPU effectively rectifies these paths, reducing attack success rate across diverse jailbreak attacks.
JPU preserves the general utility of the model on standard benchmarks.
On-policy adversarial mining is necessary for capturing dynamic attack features and ensuring robust defense.
papers.limitation: The attack buffer is primarily designed for prompt-based injection strategies, and integrating attack vectors beyond the prompt space (e.g., parameter-level manipulation) could improve robustness.
future_direction: Exploring integration of attack vectors beyond prompt space, such as parameter-level manipulation or optimization-based attacks.
papers.abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, Large Language Models (LLMs) often fail against jailbreak attacks. While machine unlearning has emerged as a promising defense by erasing specific harmful parameters, current methods remain vulnerable to diverse jailbreaks. We first conduct an empirical study and discover that this failure mechanism is caused by jailbreaks primarily activating non-erased parameters in the intermediate layers. Further, by probing the underlying mechanism through which these circumvented parameters reassemble into the prohibited output, we verify the persistent existence of dynamic $\textbf{jailbreak paths}$ and show that the inability to rectify them constitutes the fundamental gap in existing unlearning defenses. To bridge this gap, we propose $\textbf{J}$ailbreak $\textbf{P}$ath $\textbf{U}$nlearning (JPU), which is the first to rectify dynamic jailbreak paths towards safety anchors by dynamically mining on-policy adversarial samples to expose vulnerabilities and identify jailbreak paths. Extensive experiments demonstrate that JPU significantly enhances jailbreak resistance against dynamic attacks while preserving the model's utility.

papers.title: HiddenDetect: Detecting Jailbreak Attacks against Large Vision-Language Models via Monitoring Hidden States
papers.research_question: Can LVLMs detect unsafe prompts through their internal hidden states before generating any output? The paper investigates whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces HiddenDetect, a tuning-free framework that detects jailbreak attacks by monitoring refusal semantics in the hidden states of LVLMs, and shows that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns for unsafe prompts.
papers.conclusion: HiddenDetect leverages intrinsic safety signals in LVLM activations to detect jailbreak attacks without tuning, outperforming existing methods and offering a robust and scalable solution for enhancing LVLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, with refusal semantics detectable in hidden states.
Safety activation is delayed for multimodal inputs, especially when harmful intent is conveyed through images, correlating with higher attack success rates.
HiddenDetect achieves higher AUROC than existing state-of-the-art methods on both text-based and multimodal jailbreak benchmarks.
The method is tuning-free, operates directly on internal activations, and generalizes across different LVLM architectures without modification.
The most safety-aware layers are in the middle to late range, and scaling their weights increases the rejection of malicious queries.
papers.limitation:
Relies on the assumption that unsafe prompts consistently induce distinct activation patterns, which may not hold for all adversarial inputs.
Does not actively intervene in response generation, only flags unsafe prompts.
future_direction: Explore adaptive learning mechanisms to dynamically refine detection thresholds.
Integrate activation-based safety monitoring with controlled response modulation.
papers.abstract: The integration of additional modalities increases the susceptibility of large vision-language models (LVLMs) to safety risks, such as jailbreak attacks, compared to their language-only counterparts. While existing research primarily focuses on post-hoc alignment techniques, the underlying safety mechanisms within LVLMs remain largely unexplored. In this work , we investigate whether LVLMs inherently encode safety-relevant signals within their internal activations during inference. Our findings reveal that LVLMs exhibit distinct activation patterns when processing unsafe prompts, which can be leveraged to detect and mitigate adversarial inputs without requiring extensive fine-tuning. Building on this insight, we introduce HiddenDetect, a novel tuning-free framework that harnesses internal model activations to enhance safety. Experimental results show that {HiddenDetect} surpasses state-of-the-art methods in detecting jailbreak attacks against LVLMs. By utilizing intrinsic safety-aware patterns, our method provides an efficient and scalable solution for strengthening LVLM robustness against multimodal threats. Our code will be released publicly at https://github.com/leigest519/HiddenDetect.

papers.title: AdaSteer: Your Aligned LLM is Inherently an Adaptive Jailbreak Defender
papers.research_question: How can activation steering be made adaptive to input characteristics for effective jailbreak defense while preserving model utility?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts steering coefficients based on input characteristics, improving jailbreak defense while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: AdaSteer demonstrates the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies Rejection Law (R-Law): jailbreak types further against rejection direction require stronger steering.
Identifies Harmfulness Law (H-Law): jailbreak inputs shift further toward harmfulness direction compared to benign inputs.
AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods in jailbreak defense across multiple attack strategies.
AdaSteer maintains model utility on benign inputs with minimal impact.
AdaSteer is efficient and scalable across model sizes.
papers.limitation:
Tested on models up to 27B parameters; performance on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+) remains unverified.
Relies on linear activation steering, assuming model behaviors can be effectively controlled via low-dimensional vector manipulations.
future_direction: Investigating AdaSteer on larger-scale models (e.g., 30B+ parameters)
Exploring nonlinear adaptations or layer-wise adjustments to refine AdaSteer
papers.abstract: Despite extensive efforts in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Activation steering offers a training-free defense method but relies on fixed steering coefficients, resulting in suboptimal protection and increased false rejections of benign inputs. To address this, we propose AdaSteer, an adaptive activation steering method that dynamically adjusts model behavior based on input characteristics. We identify two key properties: Rejection Law (R-Law), which shows that stronger steering is needed for jailbreak inputs opposing the rejection direction, and Harmfulness Law (H-Law), which differentiates adversarial and benign inputs. AdaSteer steers input representations along both the Rejection Direction (RD) and Harmfulness Direction (HD), with adaptive coefficients learned via logistic regression, ensuring robust jailbreak defense while preserving benign input handling. Experiments on LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-2, and Qwen2.5 show that AdaSteer outperforms baseline methods across multiple jailbreak attacks with minimal impact on utility. Our results highlight the potential of interpretable model internals for real-time, flexible safety enforcement in LLMs.

papers.title: Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis
papers.research_question: How does safety alignment impact model behavior, why are safety mechanisms brittle, and can these issues be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH) and identifies safety-critical components in LLMs, showing that freezing these components during fine-tuning preserves safety without sacrificing utility.
papers.conclusion: The atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level, and safety alignment can be achieved with minimal intervention, emphasizing that safety alignment should not be complicated.
papers.key_findings:
Safety alignment teaches models to choose between fulfilling or refusing requests, akin to a binary classification task.
Only about 1.3-1.4% of model components are safety-critical (SCU).
Freezing SCUs during fine-tuning preserves safety performance.
Fine-tuning attacks convert safety-critical units to utility units, explaining brittleness.
Repurposing redundant units as an alignment budget minimizes alignment tax.
papers.limitation:
The evidence from probing experiments is necessary but not sufficient to fully capture the nuances of safety alignment.
The method is less effective on models with weaker initial safety alignment (e.g., Mistral).
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are overwhelmingly more and more integrated into various applications, ensuring they generate safe responses is a pressing need. Previous studies on alignment have largely focused on general instruction-following but have often overlooked the distinct properties of safety alignment, such as the brittleness of safety mechanisms. To bridge the gap, we propose the Superficial Safety Alignment Hypothesis (SSAH), which posits that safety alignment teaches an otherwise unsafe model to choose the correct reasoning direction - fulfill or refuse users' requests - interpreted as an implicit binary classification task. Through SSAH, we hypothesize that only a few essential components can establish safety guardrails in LLMs. We successfully identify four types of attribute-critical components: Safety Critical Unit (SCU), Utility Critical Unit (UCU), Complex Unit (CU), and Redundant Unit (RU). Our findings show that freezing certain safety-critical components during fine-tuning allows the model to retain its safety attributes while adapting to new tasks. Similarly, we show that leveraging redundant units in the pre-trained model as an "alignment budget" can effectively minimize the alignment tax while achieving the alignment goal. All considered, this paper concludes that the atomic functional unit for safety in LLMs is at the neuron level and underscores that safety alignment should not be complicated.

papers.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning
papers.research_question: How can refusal behavior in safety-aligned language models be ablated without causing collateral damage to core capabilities like math and coding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA), a method that cleans refusal vectors by orthogonalizing against capability and style directions, enabling precise ablation of refusal behavior with minimal distribution drift and preserved capabilities.
papers.conclusion: SRA treats refusal ablation as a semantic disentanglement problem, achieving behavioral editing with dramatically reduced drift and preserved capabilities compared to standard methods.
papers.key_findings:
SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0–2% on harmful suite) with negligible perplexity impact on wikitext_2_raw and minimal distribution drift.
Standard ablation induces severe distribution drift, while SRA maintains original distribution while achieving low refusal rates.
SRA preserves or improves math and code perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP datasets.
The dirty refusal vector is polysemantic, entangling refusal signals with unrelated linguistic structure and capability circuits.
Cleaning the vector via spectral residualization reduces 'Ghost Noise' damage caused by standard ablation.
papers.limitation:
The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds; unseen entanglers could still leak into the refusal direction.
Evaluation limitations include refusal detection being definition-dependent, finite harmful prompt suites, and proxy drift metrics not substituting for comprehensive behavioral evaluation.
future_direction: Automating atom discovery or expanding registries to handle unseen confounds.
papers.abstract: Safety-aligned language models systematically refuse harmful requests. While activation steering can modulate refusal, ablating the raw "refusal vector" calculated from contrastive harmful and harmless prompts often causes collateral damage and distribution drift. We argue this degradation occurs because the raw vector is polysemantic, entangling the refusal signal with core capability circuits and linguistic style. We introduce Surgical Refusal Ablation (SRA) to distill these steering directions. SRA constructs a registry of independent Concept Atoms representing protected capabilities and stylistic confounds, then uses ridge-regularized spectral residualization to orthogonalize the refusal vector against these directions. This yields a clean refusal direction that targets refusal-relevant structure while minimizing disruption to the model's semantic geometry. Across five models (Qwen3-VL and Ministral series), SRA achieves deep refusal reduction (0-2%) with negligible perplexity impact on Wikitext-2 (mean delta PPL approx. 0.02) and minimal distribution drift. Notably, standard ablation on Qwen3-VL-4B induces severe drift (first-token KL = 2.088), whereas SRA maintains the original distribution (KL = 0.044) while achieving the same 0% refusal rate. Using teacher-forced perplexity on GSM8K and MBPP as a high-resolution capability proxy, we show SRA preserves math and code distributions. These results suggest that common "model damage" is often "Ghost Noise," defined as the spectral bleeding of the dirty refusal direction into capability subspaces.

papers.title: AttnGCG: Enhancing Jailbreaking Attacks on LLMs with Attention Manipulation
papers.research_question: How can jailbreaking attacks on LLMs be enhanced by manipulating the models' attention scores?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AttnGCG, an enhanced jailbreaking attack that manipulates LLMs' attention scores to increase focus on adversarial suffixes, leading to higher attack success rates and improved transferability.
papers.conclusion: Attention manipulation is an effective strategy for enhancing jailbreaking attacks on LLMs, and visualizing attention scores offers clear insights into the attack mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
A positive correlation exists between the attention score on the adversarial suffix and the attack success rate (ASR).
AttnGCG consistently outperforms the GCG baseline across various LLMs, achieving an average ASR increase of ~6.3% (GPT-4 judge).
AttnGCG reduces the gap between keyword-based and GPT-4 judge ASR, indicating a reduction in false jailbreaks.
AttnGCG demonstrates strong transferability, improving ASR on unseen harmful goals by an average of 11.4% and on black-box LLMs like GPT-4 by 2.8%.
Attention score visualization provides interpretable insights into how jailbreaking exploits attention distributions.
papers.limitation: The transfer attack performance of AttnGCG is unsatisfactory on the latest models (Gemini-1.5-Pro-latest, Gemini-1.5-Flash, GPT-4o), necessitating further research.
future_direction: Further research to improve transfer attack performance on the latest LLM models.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the vulnerabilities of transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) to jailbreaking attacks, focusing specifically on the optimization-based Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) strategy. We first observe a positive correlation between the effectiveness of attacks and the internal behaviors of the models. For instance, attacks tend to be less effective when models pay more attention to system prompts designed to ensure LLM safety alignment. Building on this discovery, we introduce an enhanced method that manipulates models' attention scores to facilitate LLM jailbreaking, which we term AttnGCG. Empirically, AttnGCG shows consistent improvements in attack efficacy across diverse LLMs, achieving an average increase of ~7% in the Llama-2 series and ~10% in the Gemma series. Our strategy also demonstrates robust attack transferability against both unseen harmful goals and black-box LLMs like GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Moreover, we note our attention-score visualization is more interpretable, allowing us to gain better insights into how our targeted attention manipulation facilitates more effective jailbreaking. We release the code at https://github.com/UCSC-VLAA/AttnGCG-attack.

papers.title: Jailbreak Instruction-Tuned LLMs via end-of-sentence MLP Re-weighting
papers.research_question: How does re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences affect the safety mechanisms of instruction-tuned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and introduces two white-box jailbreak methods that re-weight MLP neurons to compromise safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences are critical for safety in instruction-tuned LLMs, and that re-weighting these neurons can effectively jailbreak the models, providing insights for both attack and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Re-weighting MLP neurons in end-of-sentence inferences can significantly compromise the safety of instruction-tuned LLMs.
The prompt-specific jailbreak method outperforms state-of-the-art prompt-specific methods and requires less computational time.
The prompt-general jailbreak method is comparable to state-of-the-art approaches and has minimal impact on the model's original capabilities (except for very small models).
The safety mechanism of instruction-tuned LLMs heavily relies on MLP layers in end-of-sentence inferences.
The method can also serve as a mechanism interpretability tool to identify MLP neurons strongly correlated with safety.
papers.limitation:
The method is heuristic-driven, making it more of a validation experiment rather than an optimal solution.
The precise role MLP layers play in the safety mechanism and how they impact subsequent generation processes remain open questions.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the safety mechanisms of instruction fine-tuned large language models (LLMs). We discover that re-weighting MLP neurons can significantly compromise a model's safety, especially for MLPs in end-of-sentence inferences. We hypothesize that LLMs evaluate the harmfulness of prompts during end-of-sentence inferences, and MLP layers plays a critical role in this process. Based on this hypothesis, we develop 2 novel white-box jailbreak methods: a prompt-specific method and a prompt-general method. The prompt-specific method targets individual prompts and optimizes the attack on the fly, while the prompt-general method is pre-trained offline and can generalize to unseen harmful prompts. Our methods demonstrate robust performance across 7 popular open-source LLMs, size ranging from 2B to 72B. Furthermore, our study provides insights into vulnerabilities of instruction-tuned LLM's safety and deepens the understanding of the internal mechanisms of LLMs.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Surgical, Cheap, and Flexible: Mitigating False Refusal in Language Models via Single Vector Ablation
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate false refusal in language models (where they refuse safe queries) without compromising their safety and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: A training-free, model-agnostic method that mitigates false refusal by ablating an orthogonalized false refusal vector from the model's residual stream, reducing false refusal rates while preserving safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed single vector ablation method is a surgical, cheap, and flexible approach to mitigate false refusal in language models, enabling fine-grained safety calibration without compromising general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the orthogonalized false refusal vector increases compliance on pseudo-harmful datasets while maintaining low compliance on harmful datasets.
The method has minimal impact on general model capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, Wikitext).
Partial orthogonalization allows fine-grained control over the model's refusal sensitivity via a parameter λ.
The method is computationally cheap, requiring no additional inference time or memory after weight editing.
The extracted false refusal vector generalizes to out-of-distribution pseudo-harmful test datasets.
papers.limitation:
The quality of the extracted false refusal vector depends on the diversity of the pseudo-harmful samples used for extraction.
The refusal score metric used for vector selection could be improved, e.g., by considering sequence probabilities.
future_direction: Improving the false refusal vector quality through better data curation and sampling techniques.
Developing improved evaluation metrics for refusal vector selection, such as considering sequence probabilities.
papers.abstract: Training a language model to be both helpful and harmless requires careful calibration of refusal behaviours: Models should refuse to follow malicious instructions or give harmful advice (e.g. "how do I kill someone?"), but they should not refuse safe requests, even if they superficially resemble unsafe ones (e.g. "how do I kill a Python process?"). Avoiding such false refusal, as prior work has shown, is challenging even for highly-capable language models. In this paper, we propose a simple and surgical method for mitigating false refusal in language models via single vector ablation. For a given model, we extract a false refusal vector and show that ablating this vector reduces false refusal rate without negatively impacting model safety and general model capabilities. We also show that our approach can be used for fine-grained calibration of model safety. Our approach is training-free and model-agnostic, making it useful for mitigating the problem of false refusal in current and future language models.

papers.title: The Cost of Thinking: Increased Jailbreak Risk in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Thinking mode has always been regarded as one of the most valuable modes in LLMs. However, we uncover a surprising and previously overlooked phenomenon: LLMs with thinking mode are more easily broken by Jailbreak attack. We evaluate 9 LLMs on AdvBench and HarmBench and find that the success rate of attacking thinking mode in LLMs is almost higher than that of non-thinking mode. Through large numbers of sample studies, it is found that for educational purposes and excessively long thinking lengths are the characteristics of successfully attacked data, and LLMs also give harmful answers when they mostly know that the questions are harmful. In order to alleviate the above problems, this paper proposes a method of safe thinking intervention for LLMs, which explicitly guides the internal thinking processes of LLMs by adding "specific thinking tokens" of LLMs to the prompt. The results demonstrate that the safe thinking intervention can significantly reduce the attack success rate of LLMs with thinking mode.

papers.title: Fail-Closed Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How should refusal mechanisms be structured so that safety remains effective under partial failure induced by prompt-based jailbreaks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes fail-closed alignment as a design principle and a progressive alignment framework that enforces redundant, independent refusal directions to improve robustness against jailbreaks.
papers.conclusion: Fail-closed alignment provides a principled foundation for LLM safety by enforcing redundancy in refusal mechanisms, making alignment robust to partial failure.
papers.key_findings:
Current refusal mechanisms are fail-open and depend on a single dominant direction that jailbreaks can suppress.
The proposed method reduces attack success rates by 92–97% across four jailbreak attacks.
The method achieves the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality.
Mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with the method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions.
The method generalizes to parameter-efficient settings (LoRA) with minimal performance drop.
papers.limitation: The method does not eliminate all vulnerabilities and faces attack-specific challenges, as some jailbreaks can still circumvent it in a minority of cases.
papers.abstract: We identify a structural weakness in current large language model (LLM) alignment: modern refusal mechanisms are fail-open. While existing approaches encode refusal behaviors across multiple latent features, suppressing a single dominant feature$-$via prompt-based jailbreaks$-$can cause alignment to collapse, leading to unsafe generation. Motivated by this, we propose fail-closed alignment as a design principle for robust LLM safety: refusal mechanisms should remain effective even under partial failures via redundant, independent causal pathways. We present a concrete instantiation of this principle: a progressive alignment framework that iteratively identifies and ablates previously learned refusal directions, forcing the model to reconstruct safety along new, independent subspaces. Across four jailbreak attacks, we achieve the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality, with small computational overhead. Our mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with our method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions that prompt-based jailbreaks cannot suppress simultaneously, providing empirical support for fail-closed alignment as a principled foundation for robust LLM safety.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
