papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
The harmfulness subspace formed by 55 subconcept directions is low-rank linear, with a single dominant direction capturing most of the variance.
Steering in the dominant direction allows for near elimination of harmful responses on jailbreak datasets with only a minor decrease in utility.
Linear probes for harmfulness subconcepts achieve high accuracy and generalize to out-of-distribution data.
Ablating the entire harmfulness subspace or just the dominant direction reduces jailbreak penetration with minimal utility loss.
The method works on two different models (Llama and Qwen), though with some differences in effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
The study has limited model testing and may not generalize well to other untested models of differing scales.
The subcategories of harmfulness tested are not extensive and may not include all possible subcategories of harmful model responses.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified the need to understand and reliably curb their harmful behaviours. We introduce a multidimensional framework for probing and steering harmful content in model internals. For each of 55 distinct harmfulness subconcepts (e.g., racial hate, employment scams, weapons), we learn a linear probe, yielding 55 interpretable directions in activation space. Collectively, these directions span a harmfulness subspace that we show is strikingly low-rank. We then test ablation of the entire subspace from model internals, as well as steering and ablation in the subspace's dominant direction. We find that dominant direction steering allows for near elimination of harmfulness with a low decrease in utility. Our findings advance the emerging view that concept subspaces provide a scalable lens on LLM behaviour and offer practical tools for the community to audit and harden future generations of language models.

papers.title: Surgical, Cheap, and Flexible: Mitigating False Refusal in Language Models via Single Vector Ablation
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate false refusal in language models (where they refuse safe queries) without compromising their safety and general capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: A training-free, model-agnostic method that mitigates false refusal by ablating an orthogonalized false refusal vector from the model's residual stream, reducing false refusal rates while preserving safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The proposed single vector ablation method is a surgical, cheap, and flexible approach to mitigate false refusal in language models, enabling fine-grained safety calibration without compromising general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the orthogonalized false refusal vector increases compliance on pseudo-harmful datasets while maintaining low compliance on harmful datasets.
The method has minimal impact on general model capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, Wikitext).
Partial orthogonalization allows fine-grained control over the model's refusal sensitivity via a parameter λ.
The method is computationally cheap, requiring no additional inference time or memory after weight editing.
The extracted false refusal vector generalizes to out-of-distribution pseudo-harmful test datasets.
papers.limitation:
The quality of the extracted false refusal vector depends on the diversity of the pseudo-harmful samples used for extraction.
The refusal score metric used for vector selection could be improved, e.g., by considering sequence probabilities.
future_direction: Improving the false refusal vector quality through better data curation and sampling techniques.
Developing improved evaluation metrics for refusal vector selection, such as considering sequence probabilities.
papers.abstract: Training a language model to be both helpful and harmless requires careful calibration of refusal behaviours: Models should refuse to follow malicious instructions or give harmful advice (e.g. "how do I kill someone?"), but they should not refuse safe requests, even if they superficially resemble unsafe ones (e.g. "how do I kill a Python process?"). Avoiding such false refusal, as prior work has shown, is challenging even for highly-capable language models. In this paper, we propose a simple and surgical method for mitigating false refusal in language models via single vector ablation. For a given model, we extract a false refusal vector and show that ablating this vector reduces false refusal rate without negatively impacting model safety and general model capabilities. We also show that our approach can be used for fine-grained calibration of model safety. Our approach is training-free and model-agnostic, making it useful for mitigating the problem of false refusal in current and future language models.

papers.title: The Cost of Thinking: Increased Jailbreak Risk in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Thinking mode has always been regarded as one of the most valuable modes in LLMs. However, we uncover a surprising and previously overlooked phenomenon: LLMs with thinking mode are more easily broken by Jailbreak attack. We evaluate 9 LLMs on AdvBench and HarmBench and find that the success rate of attacking thinking mode in LLMs is almost higher than that of non-thinking mode. Through large numbers of sample studies, it is found that for educational purposes and excessively long thinking lengths are the characteristics of successfully attacked data, and LLMs also give harmful answers when they mostly know that the questions are harmful. In order to alleviate the above problems, this paper proposes a method of safe thinking intervention for LLMs, which explicitly guides the internal thinking processes of LLMs by adding "specific thinking tokens" of LLMs to the prompt. The results demonstrate that the safe thinking intervention can significantly reduce the attack success rate of LLMs with thinking mode.

papers.title: Fail-Closed Alignment for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How should refusal mechanisms be structured so that safety remains effective under partial failure induced by prompt-based jailbreaks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes fail-closed alignment as a design principle and a progressive alignment framework that enforces redundant, independent refusal directions to improve robustness against jailbreaks.
papers.conclusion: Fail-closed alignment provides a principled foundation for LLM safety by enforcing redundancy in refusal mechanisms, making alignment robust to partial failure.
papers.key_findings:
Current refusal mechanisms are fail-open and depend on a single dominant direction that jailbreaks can suppress.
The proposed method reduces attack success rates by 92–97% across four jailbreak attacks.
The method achieves the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality.
Mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with the method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions.
The method generalizes to parameter-efficient settings (LoRA) with minimal performance drop.
papers.limitation: The method does not eliminate all vulnerabilities and faces attack-specific challenges, as some jailbreaks can still circumvent it in a minority of cases.
papers.abstract: We identify a structural weakness in current large language model (LLM) alignment: modern refusal mechanisms are fail-open. While existing approaches encode refusal behaviors across multiple latent features, suppressing a single dominant feature$-$via prompt-based jailbreaks$-$can cause alignment to collapse, leading to unsafe generation. Motivated by this, we propose fail-closed alignment as a design principle for robust LLM safety: refusal mechanisms should remain effective even under partial failures via redundant, independent causal pathways. We present a concrete instantiation of this principle: a progressive alignment framework that iteratively identifies and ablates previously learned refusal directions, forcing the model to reconstruct safety along new, independent subspaces. Across four jailbreak attacks, we achieve the strongest overall robustness while mitigating over-refusal and preserving generation quality, with small computational overhead. Our mechanistic analyses confirm that models trained with our method encode multiple, causally independent refusal directions that prompt-based jailbreaks cannot suppress simultaneously, providing empirical support for fail-closed alignment as a principled foundation for robust LLM safety.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: The Unintended Trade-off of AI Alignment:Balancing Hallucination Mitigation and Safety in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do truthfulness-enhancing edits affect jailbreak susceptibility, and which components mediate the truthfulness-safety interaction?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a trade-off between improving truthfulness and maintaining safety in LLMs, and proposes a method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle refusal and hallucination features, preserving the refusal subspace during fine-tuning to mitigate the trade-off.
papers.conclusion: There is a trade-off between truthfulness and refusal alignment in LLMs, and the proposed method using sparse autoencoders to disentangle features and preserve the refusal subspace during fine-tuning can maintain safety while preventing hallucinations from increasing.
papers.key_findings:
Truthfulness-enhancing edits (e.g., ITI, TruthX) increase jailbreak susceptibility, revealing a trade-off between factuality and safety.
Hallucination and refusal behaviors share overlapping internal representations in specific attention heads.
Fine-tuning on benign datasets can degrade safety alignment due to shared representational space between refusal and hallucination features.
The proposed SAE-guided fine-tuning method preserves refusal behavior while improving task utility, mitigating the trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Further investigation is needed to interpret how different alignment methods affect knowledge suppression and whether their impact varies across model architectures.
The analysis primarily examined specific components; a more comprehensive study of additional layers and mechanisms may yield deeper insights.
The proposed solution relies on a trained SAE, which may limit its practicality for fine-tuning at scale.
papers.abstract: Hallucination in large language models (LLMs) has been widely studied in recent years, with progress in both detection and mitigation aimed at improving truthfulness. Yet, a critical side effect remains largely overlooked: enhancing truthfulness can negatively impact safety alignment. In this paper, we investigate this trade-off and show that increasing factual accuracy often comes at the cost of weakened refusal behavior. Our analysis reveals that this arises from overlapping components in the model that simultaneously encode hallucination and refusal information, leading alignment methods to suppress factual knowledge unintentionally. We further examine how fine-tuning on benign datasets, even when curated for safety, can degrade alignment for the same reason. To address this, we propose a method that disentangles refusal-related features from hallucination features using sparse autoencoders, and preserves refusal behavior during fine-tuning through subspace orthogonalization. This approach prevents hallucinations from increasing while maintaining safety alignment.We evaluate our method on commonsense reasoning tasks and harmful benchmarks (AdvBench and StrongReject). Results demonstrate that our approach preserves refusal behavior and task utility, mitigating the trade-off between truthfulness and safety.

papers.title: Attention Eclipse: Manipulating Attention to Bypass LLM Safety-Alignment
papers.research_question: How can attention manipulation be used to enhance jailbreak attacks against safety-aligned LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attention Eclipse, a white-box attack framework that manipulates LLM attention mechanisms to amplify existing jailbreak techniques, improving attack success rates and reducing generation time.
papers.conclusion: Attention Eclipse highlights vulnerabilities in LLM alignment and demonstrates the need for stronger defense mechanisms against attention-based jailbreak attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Eclipse significantly improves Attack Success Rate (ASR) for jailbreak methods like GCG, AutoDAN, and ReNeLLM.
It reduces Time Cost Per Prompt (TCPP), accelerating jailbreak generation.
The attacks are transferable across models, including to closed-source LLMs like GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4o-mini.
Decomposition and attention manipulation components (φ1 and φ2) individually contribute to attack success.
Camouflaging adversarial suffixes by reducing attention on harmful content enhances jailbreak effectiveness.
papers.limitation:
Relies on access to model attention weights, making it a white-box attack.
Effectiveness depends on the quality of the initial jailbreak prompt.
Does not explicitly optimize for stealthiness against jailbreak detection systems.
future_direction: Explore other attention manipulation strategies for jailbreaks.
Investigate how attention manipulation interacts with evolving defense mechanisms.
Develop stronger alignment mechanisms to mitigate such attacks.
papers.abstract: Recent research has shown that carefully crafted jailbreak inputs can induce large language models to produce harmful outputs, despite safety measures such as alignment. It is important to anticipate the range of potential Jailbreak attacks to guide effective defenses and accurate assessment of model safety. In this paper, we present a new approach for generating highly effective Jailbreak attacks that manipulate the attention of the model to selectively strengthen or weaken attention among different parts of the prompt. By harnessing attention loss, we develop more effective jailbreak attacks, that are also transferrable. The attacks amplify the success rate of existing Jailbreak algorithms including GCG, AutoDAN, and ReNeLLM, while lowering their generation cost (for example, the amplified GCG attack achieves 91.2% ASR, vs. 67.9% for the original attack on Llama2-7B/AdvBench, using less than a third of the generation time).

papers.title: Layer-Level Self-Exposure and Patch: Affirmative Token Mitigation for Jailbreak Attack Defense
papers.research_question: How can we defend against jailbreak attacks by identifying and patching toxic layers in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Layer-AdvPatcher, a defense framework that identifies toxic layers in LLMs responsible for generating affirmative tokens to harmful prompts and patches them via adversarial augmentation and localized unlearning.
papers.conclusion: Layer-AdvPatcher effectively defends against jailbreak attacks by precisely targeting and editing toxic layers through adversarial exposure and unlearning, maintaining model utility while reducing harmful outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-AdvPatcher reduces the harmfulness and attack success rate (ASR) of jailbreak attacks without significantly compromising utility for benign queries.
Toxic layers, which exhibit a high tendency to generate affirmative tokens, are often found in the later stages of LLMs (e.g., layer 28 in Mistral, layers 21-24 in Llama2).
The method outperforms or is competitive with state-of-the-art defense strategies like Self-Examination, Paraphrase, Unlearning, and SafeDecoding.
Targeted unlearning of specific layer components (e.g., QV and LayerNorm) is more effective for defense than unlearning all parameters of a layer.
The framework is modular and can be combined with prompt-based defenses for enhanced security.
papers.limitation:
The framework has not been tested on larger models (e.g., Llama3-13B) due to computational constraints.
The selection of affirmative tokens for identifying toxic layers may not be comprehensive, affecting generalizability across models.
Open-sourcing the dataset derived from toxic layers could be misused by malicious actors to create more sophisticated attacks.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in diverse applications, including chatbot assistants and code generation, aligning their behavior with safety and ethical standards has become paramount. However, jailbreak attacks, which exploit vulnerabilities to elicit unintended or harmful outputs, threaten LLMs' safety significantly. In this paper, we introduce Layer-AdvPatcher, a novel methodology designed to defend against jailbreak attacks by utilizing an unlearning strategy to patch specific layers within LLMs through self-augmented datasets. Our insight is that certain layer(s), tend to produce affirmative tokens when faced with harmful prompts. By identifying these layers and adversarially exposing them to generate more harmful data, one can understand their inherent and diverse vulnerabilities to attacks. With these exposures, we then "unlearn" these issues, reducing the impact of affirmative tokens and hence minimizing jailbreak risks while keeping the model's responses to safe queries intact. We conduct extensive experiments on two models, four benchmark datasets, and multiple state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. Results indicate that our framework reduces the harmfulness and attack success rate of jailbreak attacks without compromising utility for benign queries compared to recent defense methods. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/oyy2000/LayerAdvPatcher

papers.title: Safety Alignment via Constrained Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the safety alignment of large language models against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving useful knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), a safety alignment method that identifies and fixes knowledge-related neurons in MLP layers during unlearning to remove harmful knowledge while preserving model utility.
papers.conclusion: CKU effectively enhances LLM safety against jailbreak attacks by unlearning harmful knowledge while preserving general capabilities, offering a promising approach for safety alignment and knowledge editing.
papers.key_findings:
CKU achieves a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods like RSFT, GAM, Eraser, Safe Unlearning, and Circuit Break.
Fixing 80% of neurons (Neuron Locking Rate=0.8) during unlearning yields the greatest safety improvement.
Unlearning applied only to a subset of MLP layers (layers 8-12) results in a fourfold increase in safety with only a 0.15% reduction in utility.
The neuron selection mechanism based on SNIP scoring is more effective than random selection for preserving utility during unlearning.
The unlearning regularization parameter λ controls the safety-utility trade-off, with λ=1.5 providing an optimal balance.
papers.limitation:
CKU's effectiveness varies across different domains or datasets.
CKU may occasionally struggle to provide nuanced explanations in highly complex or ambiguous contexts.
papers.abstract: Despite significant progress in safety alignment, large language models (LLMs) remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks. Existing defense mechanisms have not fully deleted harmful knowledge in LLMs, which allows such attacks to bypass safeguards and produce harmful outputs. To address this challenge, we propose a novel safety alignment strategy, Constrained Knowledge Unlearning (CKU), which focuses on two primary objectives: knowledge localization and retention, and unlearning harmful knowledge. CKU works by scoring neurons in specific multilayer perceptron (MLP) layers to identify a subset U of neurons associated with useful knowledge. During the unlearning process, CKU prunes the gradients of neurons in U to preserve valuable knowledge while effectively mitigating harmful content. Experimental results demonstrate that CKU significantly enhances model safety without compromising overall performance, offering a superior balance between safety and utility compared to existing methods. Additionally, our analysis of neuron knowledge sensitivity across various MLP layers provides valuable insights into the mechanics of safety alignment and model knowledge editing.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Do You Trust Me? Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in narratives, where do these representations emerge across transformer depth, how well can they be decoded, and how do they relate to psychological constructs like fairness and certainty?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in systematic, layer- and head-specific patterns that are linearly decodable and align with psychological constructs like fairness and certainty, demonstrating that trust signals emerge during pretraining without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals, offering a representational foundation for designing credible and trustworthy AI systems in web applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences between high- and low-trust narratives are observed across models, indicating trust-sensitive features emerge during pretraining.
Trustworthiness is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, with probe performance varying by layer and head.
Fine-tuning with LoRA sharpens existing trust representations rather than restructuring them.
Trust representations are most strongly associated with psychological appraisals like fairness, certainty, and accountability-self.
Nonlinear probes provide only marginal gains, indicating trust information is largely in linearly accessible subspaces.
papers.abstract: Perceived trustworthiness underpins how users navigate online information, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs),increasingly embedded in search, recommendation, and conversational systems, represent this construct in psychologically coherent ways. We analyze how instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) encode perceived trustworthiness in web-like narratives using the PEACE-Reviews dataset annotated for cognitive appraisals, emotions, and behavioral intentions. Across models, systematic layer- and head-level activation differences distinguish high- from low-trust texts, revealing that trust cues are implicitly encoded during pretraining. Probing analyses show linearly de-codable trust signals and fine-tuning effects that refine rather than restructure these representations. Strongest associations emerge with appraisals of fairness, certainty, and accountability-self -- dimensions central to human trust formation online. These findings demonstrate that modern LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals without explicit supervision, offering a representational foundation for designing credible, transparent, and trust-worthy AI systems in the web ecosystem. Code and appendix are available at: https://github.com/GerardYeo/TrustworthinessLLM.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: Attributing and Exploiting Safety Vectors through Global Optimization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can safety-critical attention heads in Large Language Models be identified through global optimization that accounts for cooperative interactions between components, and what does this reveal about the underlying safety mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GOSV, a global optimization framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads in LLMs, revealing two distinct sets of safety vectors (Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors) with low overlap, indicating separate functional pathways for safety. Based on these insights, the authors develop an inference-time jailbreak attack that outperforms existing white-box methods.
papers.conclusion: Aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety mechanisms, encoded in approximately 30% of attention heads. The GOSV framework advances mechanistic understanding of LLM safety and reveals fundamental vulnerabilities in current alignment approaches.
papers.key_findings:
GOSV identifies two spatially distinct sets of safety-critical attention heads (Malicious Injection Vectors via Harmful Patching and Safety Suppression Vectors via Zero Ablation) with consistently low overlap, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety.
Complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30% of total attention heads are repatched across all tested models, indicating that safety mechanisms are encoded in a distributed subset comprising roughly one-third of attention heads.
An inference-time jailbreak attack that repatches activations at the identified safety-critical heads achieves superior Attack Success Rates compared to existing white-box attacks, validating the effectiveness of the discovered safety vectors.
The two repatching strategies (Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation) target largely disjoint sets of attention heads, supporting the existence of distinct safety pathways rather than a unified mechanism.
Progressive intervention analysis shows that model behavior transitions from complete refusal to full harmful compliance as the number of repatched heads approaches the 30% threshold, with further intervention leading to degraded language capabilities.
papers.limitation:
No defense strategies have been developed to mitigate the identified vulnerabilities.
The approach requires white-box access for activation patching, limiting applicability to black-box scenarios.
Evaluation is limited to a set of open-source models and English-language instructions; generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors requires further investigation.
future_direction: Developing robust safeguards based on the insights from GOSV.
Extending the approach to black-box scenarios.
Investigating generalizability to larger proprietary models, multilingual contexts, and other safety-critical behaviors.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to mitigate risks, their safety guardrails remain fragile against jailbreak attacks. This reveals limited understanding of components governing safety. Existing methods rely on local, greedy attribution that assumes independent component contributions. However, they overlook the cooperative interactions between different components in LLMs, such as attention heads, which jointly contribute to safety mechanisms. We propose \textbf{G}lobal \textbf{O}ptimization for \textbf{S}afety \textbf{V}ector Extraction (GOSV), a framework that identifies safety-critical attention heads through global optimization over all heads simultaneously. We employ two complementary activation repatching strategies: Harmful Patching and Zero Ablation. These strategies identify two spatially distinct sets of safety vectors with consistently low overlap, termed Malicious Injection Vectors and Safety Suppression Vectors, demonstrating that aligned LLMs maintain separate functional pathways for safety purposes. Through systematic analyses, we find that complete safety breakdown occurs when approximately 30\% of total heads are repatched across all models. Building on these insights, we develop a novel inference-time white-box jailbreak method that exploits the identified safety vectors through activation repatching. Our attack substantially outperforms existing white-box attacks across all test models, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of the proposed GOSV framework on LLM safety interpretability.

papers.title: Model-Editing-Based Jailbreak against Safety-aligned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Is there a more stealthy jailbreak attack vector for LLMs that minimizes user involvement by directly modifying internal model structures to bypass safety alignment without input modifications?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Targeted Model Editing (TME), a white-box jailbreak method that bypasses safety filters by identifying and removing safety-critical transformations (SCTs) from MLP weight matrices, enabling harmful responses without input modifications while preserving normal model functionality.
papers.conclusion: The work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security via model editing-based jailbreaks and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
MLP activations for unsafe samples are highly consistent (due to uniform refusal), while activations for safe samples are more variable.
The difference in average activation values between safe and unsafe samples is significantly larger than the variation within unsafe samples.
The overlap rate of activated neurons between safe and unsafe inputs is low (below 25%), indicating distinct processing pathways.
The D-LLM framework, which implements TME, achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% across four open-source LLMs.
The method maintains model performance on standard benchmarks (TruthfulQA, MMLU) after editing, showing preserved functionality.
future_direction: Further unveil the vulnerabilities of D-LLM and provide insights for LLM developers to bolster safety.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed numerous fields by enabling advanced natural language interactions but remain susceptible to critical vulnerabilities, particularly jailbreak attacks. Current jailbreak techniques, while effective, often depend on input modifications, making them detectable and limiting their stealth and scalability. This paper presents Targeted Model Editing (TME), a novel white-box approach that bypasses safety filters by minimally altering internal model structures while preserving the model's intended functionalities. TME identifies and removes safety-critical transformations (SCTs) embedded in model matrices, enabling malicious queries to bypass restrictions without input modifications. By analyzing distinct activation patterns between safe and unsafe queries, TME isolates and approximates SCTs through an optimization process. Implemented in the D-LLM framework, our method achieves an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 84.86% on four mainstream open-source LLMs, maintaining high performance. Unlike existing methods, D-LLM eliminates the need for specific triggers or harmful response collections, offering a stealthier and more effective jailbreak strategy. This work reveals a covert and robust threat vector in LLM security and emphasizes the need for stronger safeguards in model safety alignment.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: SABER: Uncovering Vulnerabilities in Safety Alignment via Cross-Layer Residual Connection
papers.research_question: How can safety alignment in Large Language Models be bypassed by exploiting the layer-wise distribution of safety mechanisms and using cross-layer residual connections?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SABER, a white-box jailbreak method that uses a cross-layer residual connection to bypass safety alignment in LLMs by routing information around safety-enforcing middle-to-late layers.
papers.conclusion: SABER is an effective jailbreak method that highlights a critical vulnerability in open-source language models to subtle architectural perturbations, demonstrating that safety alignment can be circumvented via cross-layer residual connections.
papers.key_findings:
Safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers.
SABER achieves up to a 51% improvement in Attack Success Rate over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set.
SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity on benign inputs, preserving general language capabilities.
Euclidean norm-based scaling is a critical component for SABER's effectiveness.
SABER creates an alternative pathway that reduces denial responses without significantly increasing hallucinations, balancing attack success and output coherence.
papers.limitation: The outcome when more than one layer is connected is still unexplored.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) with safe-alignment training are powerful instruments with robust language comprehension capabilities. These models typically undergo meticulous alignment procedures involving human feedback to ensure the acceptance of safe inputs while rejecting harmful or unsafe ones. However, despite their massive scale and alignment efforts, LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, where malicious users manipulate the model to produce harmful outputs that it was explicitly trained to avoid. In this study, we find that the safety mechanisms in LLMs are predominantly embedded in the middle-to-late layers. Building on this insight, we introduce a novel white-box jailbreak method, SABER (Safety Alignment Bypass via Extra Residuals), which connects two intermediate layers $s$ and $e$ such that $s < e$, through a residual connection. Our approach achieves a 51% improvement over the best-performing baseline on the HarmBench test set. Furthermore, SABER induces only a marginal shift in perplexity when evaluated on the HarmBench validation set. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/PalGitts/SABER.

papers.title: Feature-Aware Malicious Output Detection and Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can we detect and mitigate malicious outputs in large language models during decoding to defend against jailbreak attacks while preserving model utility?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes FMM, a feature-aware method that detects malicious features during decoding and uses activation patching to steer the model towards refusal responses, effectively defending against jailbreak attacks while maintaining standard generation capabilities.
papers.conclusion: FMM introduces a token-level feature detection and intervention paradigm that enhances LLM safety by leveraging inherent feature extraction and rejection capabilities, offering a promising direction for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Malicious and benign output features are linearly separable in the model's hidden state space during decoding.
FMM can accurately detect malicious tokens and trigger refusal responses across various attack methods.
The method generalizes well across different large language models like LLaMA 2 and Qwen 2.
Intervention at intermediate layers (e.g., layers 12-15) is most effective for steering the model.
FMM preserves the model's utility on benign queries, as shown by maintained response and win rates on AlpacaEval.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has brought significant benefits to various domains while introducing substantial risks. Despite being fine-tuned through reinforcement learning, LLMs lack the capability to discern malicious content, limiting their defense against jailbreak. To address these safety concerns, we propose a feature-aware method for harmful response rejection (FMM), which detects the presence of malicious features within the model's feature space and adaptively adjusts the model's rejection mechanism. By employing a simple discriminator, we detect potential malicious traits during the decoding phase. Upon detecting features indicative of toxic tokens, FMM regenerates the current token. By employing activation patching, an additional rejection vector is incorporated during the subsequent token generation, steering the model towards a refusal response. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across multiple language models and diverse attack techniques, while crucially maintaining the models' standard generation capabilities.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: How large language models encode theory-of-mind: a study on sparse parameter patterns
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that these parameters are linked to RoPE positional encoding, affecting attention mechanisms and degrading ToM performance when perturbed.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that ToM capabilities in LLMs are governed by sparse, low-rank parameter patterns linked to positional encoding and attention mechanisms, providing insights into how LLMs perform social reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
An extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameter pattern exists, whose perturbation significantly affects RoPE-based models' ToM capabilities, while random perturbations do not. This degradation is linked to a reduction in contextual localization and language understanding.
The functionality of the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern relates to the positional encoding module in LLM architectures. Perturbing the pattern in LLMs with RoPE disrupts dominant frequency activations, impairing contextual localization. LLMs without RoPE lack this frequency-dependent activation structure and exhibit different sensitivity patterns.
Perturbing ToM-sensitive parameter patterns affects the attention mechanism, thereby influencing language understanding. It alters the angle between q and k_BOS under positional encoding, destabilizing the attention sink and distorting the attention matrix.
papers.limitation: The study focuses only on false-belief tasks (unexpected contents and transfer) and does not evaluate the full spectrum of ToM abilities.
future_direction: Leveraging ToM-sensitive parameters for targeted model alignment to ensure AI systems align with human ethical norms while mitigating unintended social biases.
Comparing the identified sparse parameter structures to neural representations of ToM in the human brain for comparative cognitive modeling.
Investigating if targeted attacks could degrade LLM reasoning abilities given that ToM capabilities depend on sparse and structured parameter subsets, for robustness and adversarial testing.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence of Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in large language models (LLMs) from a mechanistic perspective, focusing on the role of extremely sparse parameter patterns. We introduce a novel method to identify ToM-sensitive parameters and reveal that perturbing as little as 0.001% of these parameters significantly degrades ToM performance while also impairing contextual localization and language understanding. To understand this effect, we analyze their interactions with core architectural components of LLMs. Our findings demonstrate that these sensitive parameters are closely linked to the positional encoding module, particularly in models using Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), where perturbations disrupt dominant frequency activations critical for contextual processing. Furthermore, we show that perturbing ToM-sensitive parameters affects LLMs’ attention mechanism by modulating the angle between queries and keys under positional encoding. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal improve language model safety at inference time, and what are the trade-offs with general model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: SAE-based feature steering can improve refusal rates for unsafe prompts but introduces a systematic trade-off, degrading performance on safe prompts and general capability benchmarks, indicating deep entanglement between safety-relevant features and general language abilities.
papers.conclusion: While SAE-based feature steering is a promising, flexible approach for enhancing language model safety without retraining, its practical deployment is limited by significant trade-offs with general capabilities, highlighting the need to better understand and address feature entanglement.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal-mediating features can be identified using a simple, handcrafted prompt.
Amplifying identified SAE features (e.g., Feature 22373) increases refusal rates for unsafe prompts in both single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak settings.
This safety improvement comes with increased over-refusal on safe prompts.
Feature steering causes significant regression in factual recall (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and reasoning (GSM8K) performance, even on benign content.
Performance regressions are not unique to safety features; steering a non-safety feature (Feature 216 for philosophy) also degrades capabilities, suggesting a general limitation of the steering approach.
papers.limitation:
The feature identification method is not scalable, relying on a single handcrafted prompt.
Feature steering introduces a trade-off between improved safety and degraded performance on unrelated capabilities.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying features that mediate target behaviors.
Understanding why features are entangled with unrelated capabilities and how to isolate them.
Exploring conditional steering approaches that activate interventions only when needed.
papers.abstract: Responsible deployment of language models requires mechanisms for refusing unsafe prompts while preserving model performance. While most approaches modify model weights through additional training, we explore an alternative: steering model activations at inference time via amplifying sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal. This work uncovers a fundamental tension between SAE steering-based safety improvements and general model capabilities. While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior. This suggests that features mediating refusal may be more deeply entangled with general language model capabilities than previously understood. Our findings reveal important open questions about the nature of safety-relevant features in language models and the feasibility of isolating them for targeted intervention. While SAE-based steering shows promise as a flexible approach to enhancing language model safety, our results highlight the critical need to understand and address the mechanisms behind these capability tradeoffs before such techniques can be practically deployed.

papers.title: Activation Steering Meets Preference Optimization: Defense Against Jailbreaks in Vision Language Models
papers.research_question: How to defend against jailbreak attacks in Vision Language Models (VLMs) by combining activation steering and preference optimization to enhance safety while preserving visual understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SPO-VLM, a two-stage defense framework that combines activation steering and sequence-level preference optimization to enhance safety of VLMs against jailbreak attacks while preserving visual understanding.
papers.conclusion: SPO-VLM effectively enhances safety against jailbreak attacks while preserving visual understanding, providing a foundation for future research on activation-space intervention and preference-driven alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SPO-VLM reduces toxicity scores and attack success rates across multiple datasets and models.
SPO-VLM maintains or even improves visual understanding performance compared to baseline methods.
SPO-VLM shows transferability to unseen attack types, such as structure-based attacks.
The two-stage approach (activation steering + preference optimization) is more effective than activation steering alone.
SPO-VLM achieves a better trade-off between safety and visual understanding than prior methods like ASTRA.
future_direction: Future research on activation-space intervention and preference-driven alignment to ensure trustworthy deployment of LLMs and VLMs.
papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in integrating visual and textual information for understanding and reasoning, but remain highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. While activation steering has emerged as a promising defence, existing approaches often rely on task-specific contrastive prompts to extract harmful directions, which exhibit suboptimal performance and can degrade visual grounding performance. To address these limitations, we propose \textit{Sequence-Level Preference Optimization} for VLM (\textit{SPO-VLM}), a novel two-stage defense framework that combines activation-level intervention with policy-level optimization to enhance model robustness. In \textit{Stage I}, we compute adaptive layer-specific steering vectors from diverse data sources, enabling generalized suppression of harmful behaviors during inference. In \textit{Stage II}, we refine these steering vectors through a sequence-level preference optimization process. This stage integrates automated toxicity assessment, as well as visual-consistency rewards based on caption-image alignment, to achieve safe and semantically grounded text generation. The two-stage structure of SPO-VLM balances efficiency and effectiveness by combining a lightweight mitigation foundation in Stage I with deeper policy refinement in Stage II. Extensive experiments shown SPO-VLM enhances safety against attacks via activation steering and preference optimization, while maintaining strong performance on benign tasks without compromising visual understanding capabilities. We will release our code, model weights, and evaluation toolkit to support reproducibility and future research. \textcolor{red}{Warning: This paper may contain examples of offensive or harmful text and images.}

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: X-Boundary: Establishing Exact Safety Boundary to Shield LLMs from Multi-Turn Jailbreaks without Compromising Usability
papers.abstract: Despite the rapid development of safety alignment techniques for LLMs, defending against multi-turn jailbreaks is still a challenging task. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive comparison, revealing that some existing defense methods can improve the robustness of LLMs against multi-turn jailbreaks but compromise usability, i.e., reducing general capabilities or causing the over-refusal problem. From the perspective of mechanism interpretability of LLMs, we discover that these methods fail to establish a boundary that exactly distinguishes safe and harmful feature representations. Therefore, boundary-safe representations close to harmful representations are inevitably disrupted, leading to a decline in usability. To address this issue, we propose X-Boundary to push harmful representations away from boundary-safe representations and obtain an exact distinction boundary. In this way, harmful representations can be precisely erased without disrupting safe ones. Experimental results show that X-Boundary achieves state-of-the-art defense performance against multi-turn jailbreaks, while reducing the over-refusal rate by about 20% and maintaining nearly complete general capability. Furthermore, we theoretically prove and empirically verify that X-Boundary can accelerate the convergence process during training. Please see our code at: https://github.com/AI45Lab/X-Boundary.

papers.title: GSAE: Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders for Robust LLM Safety Steering
papers.research_question: How to effectively steer LLMs for safety by capturing distributed safety representations using graph-regularized sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAE) to capture distributed safety representations in LLMs, enabling effective runtime safety steering with high refusal rates and preserved utility.
papers.conclusion: GSAE provides a robust method for safety steering by learning distributed safety representations, achieving high safety discrimination and utility preservation across diverse models and attacks.
papers.key_findings:
GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%).
It maintains strong task accuracy on QA benchmarks (e.g., 70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K).
GSAE generalizes across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, Phi) and scales.
It is robust against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining ≥90% refusal of harmful content.
Ablation studies show that graph regularization is essential for performance, and the dual-gating mechanism enables adaptive steering.
papers.limitation: The runtime steering mechanism incurs inference latency overhead, which can interfere with optimized serving engines.
future_direction: Decomposing distributed features into interpretable safety sub-categories.
Ensuring the robustness of the neuron co-activation graph to dataset biases and adversarial inputs.
Extending graph-regularized learning to multi-modal domains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) face critical safety challenges, as they can be manipulated to generate harmful content through adversarial prompts and jailbreak attacks. Many defenses are typically either black-box guardrails that filter outputs, or internals-based methods that steer hidden activations by operationalizing safety as a single latent feature or dimension. While effective for simple concepts, this assumption is limiting, as recent evidence shows that abstract concepts such as refusal and temporality are distributed across multiple features rather than isolated in one. To address this limitation, we introduce Graph-Regularized Sparse Autoencoders (GSAEs), which extends SAEs with a Laplacian smoothness penalty on the neuron co-activation graph. Unlike standard SAEs that assign each concept to a single latent feature, GSAEs recover smooth, distributed safety representations as coherent patterns spanning multiple features. We empirically demonstrate that GSAE enables effective runtime safety steering, assembling features into a weighted set of safety-relevant directions and controlling them with a two-stage gating mechanism that activates interventions only when harmful prompts or continuations are detected during generation. This approach enforces refusals adaptively while preserving utility on benign queries. Across safety and QA benchmarks, GSAE steering achieves an average 82% selective refusal rate, substantially outperforming standard SAE steering (42%), while maintaining strong task accuracy (70% on TriviaQA, 65% on TruthfulQA, 74% on GSM8K). Robustness experiments further show generalization across LLaMA-3, Mistral, Qwen, and Phi families and resilience against jailbreak attacks (GCG, AutoDAN), consistently maintaining >= 90% refusal of harmful content.

papers.title: Cognitive Dissonance: Why Do Language Model Outputs Disagree with Internal Representations of Truthfulness?
papers.research_question: Why do language model outputs disagree with internal representations of truthfulness, and what are the different types of disagreement?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three classes of disagreement between LM outputs and internal probes—confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity—and shows that probes' superiority is often due to better calibration, and that ensembling probes and queries can improve accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that mismatches between internal and external representations of truthfulness in LMs are diverse, primarily due to different prediction pathways rather than deceptive intent, and provides a taxonomy for understanding these disagreements.
papers.key_findings:
Probes are consistently more accurate than direct queries for evaluating truthfulness in language models.
Probes are better calibrated than queries, meaning their confidence scores more accurately reflect prediction correctness.
Most disagreements between queries and probes are due to confabulation (queries confident when probes uncertain) and heterogeneity (different performance on subsets), with deception being rare.
Queries and probes are complementary, and ensembling them can further improve accuracy over using either alone.
The distribution of disagreement types varies across datasets, indicating context-dependent behavior.
papers.limitation:
Significant heterogeneity in the distribution of disagreement types across datasets, so findings may not generalize to future datasets.
Use of only a single prompt template for each experiment, which may affect the distribution of disagreements.
Presentation of only results on linear probes, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Future work may more systematically study the distribution of query–probe disagreements induced by different prompts.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) can be used to evaluate the truth of factual statements in two ways: they can be either queried for statement probabilities, or probed for internal representations of truthfulness. Past work has found that these two procedures sometimes disagree, and that probes tend to be more accurate than LM outputs. This has led some researchers to conclude that LMs “lie’ or otherwise encode non-cooperative communicative intents. Is this an accurate description of today’s LMs, or can query–probe disagreement arise in other ways? We identify three different classes of disagreement, which we term confabulation, deception, and heterogeneity. In many cases, the superiority of probes is simply attributable to better calibration on uncertain answers rather than a greater fraction of correct, high-confidence answers. In some cases, queries and probes perform better on different subsets of inputs, and accuracy can further be improved by ensembling the two.

papers.title: One Leak Away: How Pretrained Model Exposure Amplifies Jailbreak Risks in Finetuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Do finetuned LLMs inherit the jailbreak vulnerabilities of their pretrained counterparts, and can attackers exploit knowledge of the pretrained model to launch more effective jailbreak attacks against finetuned systems?
papers.core_contribution: Finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and the proposed Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack leverages representation-level signals in the pretrained model to craft highly transferable adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: Finetuned LLMs inherit vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and publicly releasing pretrained checkpoints increases the security risks for downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts crafted on a pretrained LLM transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, indicating inherited vulnerabilities.
Transferable jailbreak prompts are linearly separable in the pretrained LLM's hidden representations, showing transferability is encoded in the feature space.
The proposed PGP attack consistently outperforms existing methods in the pretrain-to-finetune threat setting.
PGP remains effective even when the finetuned model has undergone safety tuning.
Attack success is highly dependent on using the correct pretrained source model; using a different pretrained model yields near-zero transferability.
papers.limitation: The paper does not propose a defense to mitigate the inherited vulnerabilities.
future_direction: Design methods that prevent or reduce the inheritance of vulnerabilities during finetuning.
papers.abstract: Finetuning pretrained large language models (LLMs) has become the standard paradigm for developing downstream applications. However, its security implications remain unclear, particularly regarding whether finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained sources. We investigate this question in a realistic pretrain-to-finetune threat model, where the attacker has white-box access to the pretrained LLM and only black-box access to its finetuned derivatives. Empirical analysis shows that adversarial prompts optimized on the pretrained model transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, revealing inherited vulnerabilities from pretrained to finetuned LLMs. To further examine this inheritance, we conduct representation-level probing, which shows that transferable prompts are linearly separable within the pretrained hidden states, suggesting that universal transferability is encoded in pretrained representations.
